question: A screening procedure for detecting hemoglobin F is the:
explanation:
The Kleihauer-Betke procedure is commonly used as a screening test to determine the
amount of fetal blood that has mixed with maternal blood. Blood smears are immersed in
an acid buffer, which causes HgA to be eluted form the RBCs. The smear is stained and the
RBCs that contain fetal hemoglobin take up the stain. This stain can be used in assessing
hereditary persistence of fetal hemoglobin (HPFH), fetal maternal hemorrhage, and beta
thalassemia.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.10.10.3) [Rodak 2020, p858]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 297 · boc2 PDF page 2

question: The Prussian blue staining of peripheral blood identifies:
explanation:
Siderocytes (and sideroblasts) may be identified with the Prussian blue iron stain, which
stains iron deposits. Siderocytes are RBCs that have no nuclei but contain iron. When the iron
surrounds the nucleus of immature RBCs, the cells are called ringed sideroblasts.
[Rodak 2020, p273]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 298 · boc2 PDF page 2

question: Which of the following stains is used to demonstrate iron, ferritin and hemosiderin?
explanation:
The Prussian blue stain is used for assessing iron stores in bone marrow.Prussian blue is
considered the gold standard for the assessment of iron stores.
[QCMLS 2021 4.10.5.2) [Rodak 2020, p111]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 299 · boc2 PDF page 2

question:
Which of the following stains can be used to differentiate siderotic granules
(Pappenheimer bodies) from basophilic stippling?
explanation:
The Prussian blue stain is used to differentiate siderotic (iron) granules (Pappenheimer
bodies) from basophilic stippling. The term "Pappenheimer" describes these granules when
viewed in RBCs with a Wright stain. The term "siderocyte" describes the granules in RBCs
when Prussian blue is used. Pappenheimer bodies are composed of iron; basophilic stipping
is composed of precipitated RNA.
(QCMLS 2021: 14.18] [Rodak 2020, p256 116.3]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 300 · boc2 PDF page 2

question: Which cell type shows the most intense staining with myeloperoxidase?
explanation:
Myeloperoxidase (MPO) is an enzyme found in the primary granules of granulocytic cells.
Lymphocytes do not exhibit MPO. The stain is used to differentiate AML from ALL.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.10.10.1) [Rodak 2020, p549]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 301 · boc2 PDF page 3

question: Which substrate is used for the detection of specific esterase?
explanation:
Esterases are used to differentiate myeloblasts from cells of monocytic origin.
Alpha-naphthyl acetate and alpha-naphthyl butyrate are nonspecific esterases. Naphthol
AS-D chloroacetate is a specific esterase, which means that only granulocytic cells show
staining. The nonspecific esterase stains monocytic cells, while granulocytes are negative.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.10.10.1] [Rodak 2020, p550]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 302 · boc2 PDF page 3

question:
A myeloperoxidase stain and immunophenotyping are performed on bone marrow smears
from a patient diagnosed with an acute leukemia. The myeloperoxidase is positive and
immunophenotyping shows positivity for CD4, CD13, CD11b, CD13, CD33 and CD64.
What type of leukemia is indicated?
explanation:
Myeloperoxidase is positive, along with chloroacetate, both of which are granulocytic
markers. Alpha-naphthyl acetate is also positive and indicates cells of monocytic origin are
present. Blasts that are positive for all the stains suggest the presence of both myeloblasts
and monoblasts, or the diagnosis of a myelomonocytic leukemia.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.10.10.1) [Rodak 2020, p549-551)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 303 · boc2 PDF page 3

question:
Which of the following stains is closely associated with the lysosomal enzyme in primary
(azurophilic) granules?
explanation:
Myeloperoxidase (MPO) is an enzyme found in the primary granules of granulocytic cells.
Lymphocytes do not exhibit MPO. The stain is used to differentiate AML from ALL.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.10.10.1) (Rodak 2020, p549)
H. Other Studies
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 304 · boc2 PDF page 3

question: Heinz bodies are:
explanation:
The composition of Heinz bodies is denatured hemoglobin; these inclusions and are not
seen with Wright stain. They are associated with a G6PD deficiency.
(QCMLS 2021: 4.10.10.4) [Rodak 2020, p256)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 305 · boc2 PDF page 3

question:
Which of the following technical factors will cause a normal (low) erythrocyte sedimentation
rate?
options: small fibrin clots in the sample
explanation:
Specimen handling and technical factors can affect the ESR. A clotted specimen and
delay in testing will decrease the ESR.
[Rodak 2020, p168-169]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 306 · boc2 PDF page 3

question: The erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) can be falsely elevated by:
explanation:
A falsely-elevated ESR can be caused by high room temperature, tilting of the tube,
and vibration.
[Rodak 2020, p168-169)
/. Flow Cytometry lmmunophenotyping
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 307 · boc2 PDF page 3

question: A confirmatory test for paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria is:
explanation:
PNH is an acquired clonal hematopoietic stem cell disorder; it results in a rare, chronic,
intravascular hemolytic anemia. Blood cell membranes are missing GPl-anchored proteins
designated CD55 and CD59. Absence of these proteins causes the RBCs to be lysed by
complement. lnmmunophenotyping is the confirmatory testing method and typically uses
fluorescent monoclonal antibodies to demonstrate the GPl-anchored proteins.
[QCMLS 2021 : 4.7.1.3.1.1) [Rodak 2020, p347-354]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 308 · boc2 PDF page 3

question:
Which of the following test results are consistent with a diagnosis of paroxysmal nocturnal
hemoglobinuria (PNH)?
options: decreased conversion of NADH to NAO
explanation:
Blood cell membranes are missing GPl-anchored proteins, ie, CD55 and CD59.
lmmunophenotyping by flow cytometry shows diminished staining for CD55.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.7.1.3.1.1) [Rodak 2020, p347-354)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 309 · boc2 PDF page 4

question: Terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT) is a marker found on:
explanation:
Terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT) is a marker for precursor B and T-cell ALL.
[QCMLS 2021 : 4.10.12) [Rodak 2020, p483]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 310 · boc2 PDF page 4

question: In which of the following types of cells is CD5 usually expressed?
explanation:
CD surface markers that identify mature (post-thymic) T cells include CDS.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.10.12) [Rodak 2020, p483)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 311 · boc2 PDF page 4

question:
Bone marrow examination reveals a hypercellular marrow consisting of probable
lymphoblasts. The cells are positive for TdT, CD3 and CD?; however, the lymphoblasts
are negative for surface immunoglobulins, CD19, and CD10 (CALLA). The most likely
diagnosis is:
explanation:
T-cell markers include CD34, CO2, CD3, CD4, CDS, CD7, CD8 and TOT. B-cell markers
include CD34, CD10, CD19, HLA-DR,TDT, and surface immunoglobulin.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.10.12) [Rodak 2020, p347-354)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 312 · boc2 PDF page 4

question:
A cell surface marker that is expressed on neoplastic plasma cells and is helpful in the
diagnosis of myeloma is:
explanation:
CD138, or kappa and lambda clonal excess, is useful in delineating malignant plasma
cells from a reactive process. Multiple myeloma is a bone marrow based disease in which
plasma cells are found in the marrow. This disorder also presents with a monoclonial protein
or M spike, representing the immunoglobin portion of protein electrophoresis.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.9.6.2.4) [Rodak 2020, p619-620)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 313 · boc2 PDF page 4

question: Which of the following markers are usually negative in hairy cell leukemia?
explanation:
Hairy cells are mature B lymphocytes that are positive for CD markers CD19, CD20,
CD22, CD25, CD11c, CD103, surface immunoglobulin and TRAP. CDS is a T-cell marker.
[QCMLS 2021 : 4.9.6.1.3] [Rodak 2020, p611-612]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 314 · boc2 PDF page 4

question: Which of the following markers is expressed in most cases of AML?
explanation:
CD117 is one of several markers that will be positive in most cases of AML.
Others include CD13, CD15, CD33 and CD64.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.9.1.2, 14.9) [Rodak 2020, p483]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 315 · boc2 PDF page 4

question: What feature do CD markers define in a cell?
explanation:
Clusters of differentiation (CD) markers are cellular antigens. Most are determined by flow
cytometry and are instrumental in determining the particular cell's lineage in a blood disorder.
(QCMLS 2021: 4.10.12] [McKenzie 2020, p998)
J. Molecular and Cytogenetic Testing
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 316 · boc2 PDF page 4

question: Which of the following conditions is most often associated with the V617F mutation of JAK2?
explanation:
The specific JAK2 mutation is detected in 95% of patients with polycythemia vera (PV),
which is a myleloproliferative neoplasm with elevations seen in all 3 cell lines.
[QCMLS 2021: 14.11] [Rodak 2020, p565-572]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 317 · boc2 PDF page 5

question:
The t(8;14) chromosomal translocation brings which of the following 2 genes in close
~v proximity?
options: core binding factor alpha and the retinoic acid receptor
the Abelson tyrosine kinase and breakpoint cluster region
c-myc and the immunoglobulin heavy chain
core binding factor beta and the myosin heavy chain
explanation:
The t(8;14) typically found in Burkitt leukemia brings the master cell cycle control factor
c-myc on chromosome 8 under the influence of the strong immunoglobulin heavy chain
promoter on chromosome 14, driving a leukemogenic process.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.9.7.2]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 318 · boc2 PDF page 5

question:
Which condition is associated with the BCR/ABL gene rearrangement and responds well to
treatment with tyrosine kinase inhibitors?
explanation:
The BCRIABL gene rearrangement is seen in CML. Use of tyrosine kinase inhibitors
results in prolonged survival in most patients with this leukemia and is the first treatment
option, except in pregnant patients.
[QCMLS 4.9.3.1.2.1; 14.11] [McKenzie 2020, p528]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 319 · boc2 PDF page 5

question:
This AML with recurrent cytogenetic abnormality often presents with disseminated
intravascular coagulation:
explanation:
Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) is often the presenting condition in
patients eventually diagnosed with the 1(15; 17) translocation. This AML is also known
as acute promyelocytic leukemia. Most patients respond well to targeted therapy with
all-trans-retinoic acid (ATRA).
[QCMLS 4.9.1.2; 14.9]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 320 · boc2 PDF page 5

question: Vasoconstriction is caused by several regulatory molecules, which include:
explanation:
Thromboxane A2 promotes platelet aggregation and vasoconstriction. Serotonin released
from the dense bodies of platelets is a vasoconstrictor that binds endothelial cells and platelet
membranes.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.2.1) [Rodak 2020, p143, 631]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 1 · boc2 PDF page 36

question:
Warfarin is classified as a vitamin K antagonist. The factors that are impacted by warfarin
therapy are:
explanation:
Warfarin interferes with the carboxylation of vitamin K factors by interrupting the
enzymatic phase of the reaction. Factors are inhibited according to their half life, with VII
having the shortest (6 hours) and II the longest (2-3 days).
[QCMLS 2021 : 5.7.5.1.1] (Rodak 2020, p748-749]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 2 · boc2 PDF page 36

question: When a patient is placed on warfarin therapy, the first factor that will be decreased is:
explanation:
Factor VII (proconvertin) is a single-chain glycoprotein that is vitamin-K-dependent
and remains stable for 6 hours in blood. Produced in the liver, it has the shortest half-life;
therefore, it is the first factor affected when a vitamin K antagonist such as warfarin is
administered. FIi has the longest half-life (2-3) days and FVIII is not impacted by warfarin.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.7.5.1.1) [Rodak 2020, p748-749]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 3 · boc2 PDF page 36

question:
A patient with a positive family history of bleeding presents to the ED with the results shown
in this table:
test
result
reference range
aPTT
29.5 seconds
25-35 seconds
PT
19.2 seconds
10.5-12.5 seconds
The patient is not on any medication and so is likely to be deficient in factor:
explanation:
The extrinsic pathway is initiated by the release of tissue thromboplastin that has been
expressed after damage to a vessel. During this process factor VII forms a complex with
tissue thromboplastin and calcium. The PT will be abnormal with deficiencies in the factors
found in both the extrinsic (FVII) and common pathways (I. 11, V and X) and the aPTT is
abnormal when there are deficiencies in the intrinsic pathway (FVIII, FIX, FXI and FXII).
Deficiencies in the intrinsic pathway prevent the activation of factor X in the common pathway
resulting in a prolongation of the aPTT. Factors II and V are found in the common pathway,
and factor VIII is in the intrinsic pathway. Since the aPTT is normal in this case, the likely
deficiency is in factor VII.
(QCMLS 2021 : 5.6.1.2) [Kottke-Marchant 2016, p9, 176)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 4 · boc2 PDF page 36

question: Hageman factor (XII) is involved in each of the following reactions except:
options: activation of C1 to C1 esterase
explanation:
Factor XII is a contact factor, which is activated to factor Xlla. Factor Xlla is responsible
for the activation of factor XI to factor Xia and the conversion of plasminogen to plasm in.
Fibrinogen is converted to fibrin by the action of thrombin.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.4.3, 15.3) [Kottke-Marchant 2016, p10, 35]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 5 · boc2 PDF page 36

question: The most potent plasminogen activator in the contact phase of coagulation is:
explanation:
A clot is degraded by plasmin in the fibrinolytic system. Plasminogen is the zymogen
produced when factor Xlla and kallikrein are produced by contact activation.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.4.4) [Kottke-Marchant 2016, p48)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 6 · boc2 PDF page 37

question: The activation of plasminogen to plasmin resulting in the degradation of fibrin occurs by:
explanation:
The dissolution of clots occurs several hours after the clot is formed and the key
component is plasminogen. This is converted to plasmin through TPA. This substance is
released as a result of the activity of endothelial damage and the production of thrombin.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.4.4, 15.4)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 7 · boc2 PDF page 37

question: How does tissue factor pathway inhibitor inhibit coagulation?
options: inhibition of tissue factor-factor VI la-factor Xa complex
uncoupling factor XIII dependent crosslinking of fibrin
binding and hiding tissue factor on the endothelial surface
explanation:
TFP1 , also known as extrinsic pathway inhibitor, functions predominantly by inhibiting
the critical first step of coagulation, the formation of the tissue factor-factor VIia-factor Xa
complex.
(QCMLS 2021 : 5.4.2, 15.3]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 8 · boc2 PDF page 37

question: An inhibitor of plasmin activity is:
explanation:
Alpha-2 antiplasmin is synthesized in the liver and is the primary inhibitor of free plasmin.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.4.4, 15.4] [Rodak 2020, p644]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 9 · boc2 PDF page 37

question: Antithrombin inhibits factors:
explanation:
AT is a serine protease inhibitor that bin_ds and neutralizes serine proteases, including
thrombin (FIia) and factors IXa, Xa, Xia, and Xlla.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.7.2.1] (Rodak 2020, p642]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 10 · boc2 PDF page 37

question: The propagation phase of the in vivo coagulation model includes:
options: activation of factor Va and factor VIiia
explanation:
During propagation, 95% of thrombin generation occurs. In the initiation phase, platelets
are activated by the low levels of thrombin that are generated, and adhere to exposed
collagen. The cofactors Va and VIiia are activated by thrombin during the initiation phase.
(QCMLS 2021: 5.4.3] [Rodak 2020, p640]
~ - - - - -
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 11 · boc2 PDF page 37

question: In the cell-based model of coagulation the intrinsic pathway operates on the:
options: activated platelet surface to produce the burst of thrombin
tissue factor bearing cell to initiate and amplify coagulation
explanation:
In the cell based model of coagulation, the extrinsic or tissue factor pathway operates on
the tissue factor-bearing cell and the intrinsic pathway as occurring on the platelet surface.
(QCMLS 2021 : 5.4.3] [Rodak 2020, p640]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 12 · boc2 PDF page 37

question:
A new oral anticoagulant apixaban has been given to a patient who was previously on
warfarin. This drug directly inhibits:
explanation:
Apixaban is an oral direct anti-FXa inhibitor used to prevent VTE. Direct thrombin
inhibitors will inhibit factor Ila, vitamin K antagonists inhibit the vitamin-K-dependent factors,
while LMWH can inhibit both Ila and Xa.
(QCMLS 2021: 5.7.5.1.2] [Rodak 2020, p747-754]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 13 · boc2 PDF page 37

question: The anticoagulant that directly inhibits thrombin is:
explanation:
Argatroban is a direct thrombin inhibitor that reversibly binds and inactivated free and
clot-bound thrombin. LMWH will inhibit both factor Ila and Xa, whereas warfarin inhibits
vitamin-K-dependent factors. Rivorxaban is an oral direct anti-Xa inhibitor.
[QCMLS 2021 : 5.7.5.2.2] [Rodak 2020, p757-758]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 14 · boc2 PDF page 37

question:
A patient who presents with renal impairment is being started on oral anticoagulant therapy.
The DOAC that should be avoided would be:
Ml s
explanation:
The drug dabigatran is cleared by the kidneys with a half-life of 12-17 hours; however, in
renal disease the half-life may be prolonged up to 60 hours and cause an overdose. Apixaban
and rivaroxaban is only partially eliminated by the kidney, warfarin is eliminated hepatically.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.7.5.1.2.2] [Rodak 2020, p756-757]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 15 · boc2 PDF page 38

question:
In secondary hemostasis, coagulation proteins become activated to form a fibrin clot. Prior to
these proteins being activated, their inactive proenzymes are known as:
explanation:
In secondary hemostasis, serine proteases are activated to form a fibrin clot. These
proenzymes circulate as zymogens. Zymogens are an inactive protein precursor of an
enzyme converted into an active form.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.4.1, 15.2] [Rodak 2020, p631-632]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 16 · boc2 PDF page 38

question: Alpha granules are found on the platelet in the:
explanation:
The peripheral zone is associated with platelet adhesion and aggregation. The sol-gel
zone provides a cytoskeletal system. The organelle zone contains alpha, dense, and
lysosome granules. Membranes contain the dense tubular system.
(QCMLS 2021: 5.3.1, f5.1]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 17 · boc2 PDF page 38

question: Which of the following best represents the 3 steps of normal hemostasis (in order)?
options: decreased heart rate, adhesion of platelets, plug formation
platelet aggregation, formation of FXIII, fibrin plug
explanation:
Initially vascular damage is met with the body's reaction of "clamping down" to avoid
further blood loss. This usually takes the form of vasoconstriction. In response platelets
adhere to vessels and then aggregate with each other. The primitive platelet plug is then
replaced by the fibrin clot produced through the action of the clotting cascade.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.1, 5.3.2]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 18 · boc2 PDF page 38

question: Which of the following platelet antigens is the receptor for collagen?
explanation:
All of the glycoprotein complexes are receptors for extracellular antigens. GPlbN/IX is the
vWF receptor, GPllb/llla is the fibrinogen receptor, and GPla/lla is the collagen receptor.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.3.3, f5.2, 15.1] (Kottke-Marchant 2016, p20-21]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 19 · boc2 PDF page 38

question: Which platelet surface antigen acts as the receptor for fibrinogen?
explanation:
The GPlbN/IX complex (CD42) serves as the receptor for platelet adhesion by binding
with von Willebrand factor (vWF). This is followed by GPllb/llla which assists with platelet
aggregation through the binding of fibrinogen. Deficiencies in GPlb lead to Bernard-Soulier
syndrome while a mutation of GPllb/llla accounts for the weakened ("thrombasthenia")
platelet binding in Glanzmann thrombasthenia.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.3.3, f5.2, 15.1] [Kottke-Marchant 2016, p22-23, 213-218]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 20 · boc2 PDF page 38

question: How does GPlb become activated in vivo and in vitro, respectively?
explanation:
GPlb along with GPV/IX acts as a receptor for vWF on the exposed basement membrane
of the endothelium. Shear forces from the circulation activate GPlb in vivo. Ristocetin is an
antibiotic with the side effect of promoting platelet adhesion and will activate GP1 b in vitro.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.3.3] [Kottke-Marchant 2016, p20]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 21 · boc2 PDF page 38

question:
A patient is on aspirin 100 mg/day to prevent the formation of clots caused by platelets.
The mechanism in which aspirin impairs platelet function is by:
options: inactivating cyclooxygenase which blocks thromboxane A2
impairs vWF by via GPlb/lXN receptor
inactivation of ADP and phospholipase A2
explanation:
The acetylation of aspirin inactivates cyclooxygenase, which blocks thromboxane A2
production, which causes impaired platelet function.
[QCMLS 2021 : 5.7.5.2.1, 15.13]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 22 · boc2 PDF page 38

question: A patient is diagnosed with a factor V Leiden mutation. The factor V activity level should be:
explanation:
The Factor V Leiden mutation has no effect on the procoagulant activity of Factor V.
The activity of FV should be within the reference range.
[QCMLS 2021 : 5.7.2.4] [Rodak 2020, p728]
- - - - - -
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 23 · boc2 PDF page 38

question:
The International Sensitivity Index (ISi) is determined by comparing the PT results of the
manufacturer's reagent against:
explanation:
Human brain thromboplastin is the most sensitive of reagents and assigned an ISi of 1.0.
Manufacturers compare their reagents to the most sensitive reagent to determine their
reagents ISi. Micronized silica is an activator in aPTT reagents, rabbit thromboplastin is a type
of PT reagent.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.8.2.2] [Rodak 2020, p750)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 24 · boc2 PDF page 39

question:
A coagulation reagent should be sensitive to factor deficiencies. A reagent is considered
sensitive to a factor when the level of factor activity is approximately:
explanation:
A coagulation reagent is considered sensitive to a factor deficiency if it is prolonged when
a patient's factor level is less than 30%, this is the level that will cause most patients to bleed.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.8.2.3] [Rodak 2020, p749]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 25 · boc2 PDF page 39

question: What factors are considered heat labile?
explanation:
Factors V and VIII are considered heat labile and are not stable.
[QCMLS 2021: t.5.2]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 26 · boc2 PDF page 39

question: What factor serves as a carrier for factor VIII?
explanation:
vWF serves as a carrier for factor VIII. It protects FVIII in circulation and it co-localizes
FVIII at the cite of vascular injury.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.5.2.3] [Rodak 2020, p659]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 27 · boc2 PDF page 39

question: Patients may present with either a bleeding or a thrombotic event in:
explanation:
In a dysfibrinogenemia, the fibrinogen molecule is dysfunctional and can cause either
clotting or bleeding. In hypofibrinogenemia patients present with low fibrinogen, and
in a fibrinogenemia patients have absent fibrinogen, both are at a risk for bleeding. In
hyperfibrinogenemia, there are elevated levels of fibrinogen, if these levels are persistently
high it could put a patient at a risk for thrombosis.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.6.1.3]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 28 · boc2 PDF page 39

question: The key enzyme of the fibrinolytic system is:
explanation:
Plasmin if the key enzyme responsible for the breakdown of clots. Thrombin is the
key enzyme in the formation of clots. Both urokinase and streptokinase are activators of
fibrinolysis.
[QCMLS 2021 : 5.4.4]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 29 · boc2 PDF page 39

question: The major serine protease responsible for clot breakdown is:
explanation:
Tissue plasminogen activator is a serine protease that catalyzes the conversion of
plasminogen to plasmin and is responsible for clot breakdown. Alpha-2 antiplasmin inactivates
plasmin and plasminogen activator inhibitor inhibits the plasminogen activators. Streptokinase
is a fibrinolytic used to breakdown clots.
[QCMLS 2021 : 5.4.4]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 30 · boc2 PDF page 39

question: What subendothelial structural protein triggers coagulation through activation of FVII?
explanation:
Factor VII is activated in the coagulation cascade by tissue factor. Silica is an activator for
the aPTT.
(QCMLS 2021: 5.4.2]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 31 · boc2 PDF page 39

question: Protein C and its cofactor protein S proteolytically inactivate factors:
explanation:
Factor Va and VIiia inactivation leads to a thrombotic condition. Factors Ila and Xa are
inactivated by AT.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.7.2.2]
II. Disease States
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 32 · boc2 PDF page 39

question: Arterial thrombosis is caused by:
explanation:
Activated platelets, monocytes, and macrophages become embedded within fatty plaque
combining with vWF to form arterial platelet plugs resulting in "white" thrombi seen in arterial
thrombosis, while venous thrombosis is caused by fibrin and RBC.
(QCMLS 2021: 5.7.1.2) [Rodak 2020, p721)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 33 · boc2 PDF page 40

question: The 2 factors that differentiate liver disease from vitamin K deficiency are:
explanation:
Factors V and VII are helpful in distinguishing between liver disease and vitamin K
deficiency. FVII is a vitamin-K-dependent factor; however, FV is not and will not be decreased
with a vitamin K deficiency. Both factors will be decreased in liver disease.
(QCMLS 2021: 5.6.2.4) [Rodak 2020, p654]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 34 · boc2 PDF page 40

question:
In a patient diagnosed with liver disease, which one of the following factors typically shows an
increase?
explanation:
Liver disease causes a decrease in all factors produced in the liver (factors 11, V, VII, IX,
and X); since FVIII is predominantly produced in endothelial cells, it is not decreased. It also
is an acute phase reactant that may be elevated in liver disease.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.6.2.2] [Rodak 2020, p654]
- - - - - -
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 35 · boc2 PDF page 40

question:
A 4-year-old boy presents with chronic ear infections and is on prophylactic antibiotics. He
also presents with a bleeding diathesis. Factor assay results are shown in this table:
test
patient result
reference range
factor VIII
100%
50-150%
factor V
75%
50-150%
factor IX
38%
50-150%
factor II
22%
50-150%
Possible causes are:
explanation:
Long-term antibiotic therapy disrupts normal flora, which provide a source of vitamin K
synthesis. This results in a vitamin K deficiency (11, VII, IX and X). Factors V and VIII are
vitamin K independent factors and, as such, would be within the reference range.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.6.2.4] [Rodak 2020, p656]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 36 · boc2 PDF page 40

question: A hemophiliac male and a normal female can produce a:
explanation:
All daughters of hemophiliac men are carriers of the disease; all sons are normal.

explanation:

,.n.s

explanation:
An antibody against factor VIII presents as a prolongation of the aPTT with a relatively
normal PT due to the fact that factor VIII is required for the activation of factor X in the intrinsic

[QCMLS 2021: 5.8.3.3.2] [Rodak 2020, p633, 637-638]

question: What is usually the factor VIII level in a hemophiliac patient with spontaneous bleeding?
explanation:
For spontaneous bleeding to occur, there must be a severe deficiency of FVIII. Even small
amounts of FVIII are protective. Patients with FVlll levels of 5-10% will only present with
excessive bleeding following trauma or surgery. The aPTT as a screen is relatively insensitive
in detecting FVIII deficiency. Most reagents demonstrate normal aPTT values until there is
<30% of factor VIII levels.
[QCMLS 2021 : 5.6.1.1.2, 15.9] [Rodak 2020, p664]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 45 · boc2 PDF page 42

question: What is the most common presentation of factor XIII deficiency?
options: severe bleeding not responsive to DDAVP
explanation:
Factor XIII deficiency causes a mild bleeding disorder where patients initially clot but
later start to bleed. This makes sense in respect to the role of FXIII in the stabilization of the
formed clot.
(QCMLS 2021: 5.8.2.1] [Rodak 2020, p637, 668]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 46 · boc2 PDF page 42

question: A patient is diagnosed with amyloidosis, they will be deficient in which of the following factors?
explanation:
Amyloid fibrils in the vasculature can selectively adsorb factor X leading to an acquired
factor X deficiency. It presents with a prolonged PT and PTT since FX is in the common
pathway, which corrects with mixing studies.
[QCMLS 2021 : 5.6.2, 15.1 OJ [Rodak 2020, p668]
- - - - - -
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 47 · boc2 PDF page 42

question: Which of the following tests are the most beneficial tool to aid in the diagnosis of DIC?
explanation:
No single test is specific for DIC, but rather a combination of tests is used to aid in
establishing a diagnosis. However, all of these tests will be impacted in DIC.
[QCMLS 2021 : 5.6.2.3.1) [Rodak 2020, p735]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 48 · boc2 PDF page 42

A patient that has a lupus anticoagulant may bleed due to:
MlS

question: Patients with factor XIII deficiency have:
explanation:
Adults with factor XIII (fibrin stabilizing factor) deficiency experience slow but progressive
bleeding accompanied by poor would healing and slowly resolving hematomas. A congenital
deficiency in infants involves seepage at the umbilical stump.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.6.1.2) [Rodak 2020, p668)

question: In hemolytic disease of the newborn, babies present with:
explanation:
In HDNB neonates present with decreased hemoglobin, increased reticulocyte count, and
increased level of serum indirect bilirubin.
[QCMLS 2021 : 5.6.2.5) (Rodak 2020, p388)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 52 · boc2 PDF page 43

question: Occasional spontaneous bleeding may occur in a hemophiliac who is classified as:
explanation:
Occasional spontaneous bleeding is seen in moderate hemophilia (1-5% FVIII), while
frequent spontaneous bleeding is seen in severe hemophilia (<1% FVIII).
[QCMLS 2021: 5.6.1.1, 15.9] [Rodak 2020, p664)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 53 · boc2 PDF page 43

question: In liver disease patients present with decreased synthesis of:
explanation:
Coagulation factors are produced in the liver, (some of factor VIII is made in endothelial
cells) therefore liver disease alters the production of the vitamin-K-dependent factors (11, VII,
IX, X, proteins C, S, and Z).
[QCMLS 2021 : 5.6.2.2] [Rodak 2020, p654)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 54 · boc2 PDF page 43

question: Alloantibodies are found in:
explanation:
Alloantibodies arise in response to treatment, 30% of patients with severe hemophilia
and 3% of those with moderate hemophilia. Autoantibodies are found in acquired hemophilia.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.6.2.1] [Rodak 2020, p657]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 55 · boc2 PDF page 43

question:
When there is a disparity between the results of the fibrinogen antigen and the activity, the
most likely diagnosis is:
explanation:
Dysfibrinogenemia is caused by a structurally abnormal fibrinogen. The diagnosis is
confirmed by demonstrating a low fibrinogen activity to fibrinogen antigen ratio as well as an
elevated thrombin time and a prolonged reptilase time.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.6.1.3] [Kottke-Marchant 2016, p190)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 56 · boc2 PDF page 43

question: Bleeding doesn't correlate well with factor levels in a deficiency of:
explanation:
Factor XI supplements or boosts the activation of Factor IX, so deficiencies of factor XI
are less severe clinically than deficiencies of factors IX or VIII.
[QCMLS 2021 : 5.6.1.1.3) (Rodak 2016, p667]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 57 · boc2 PDF page 43

question:
A newborn baby boy is known to have a homozygous protein C deficiency. This puts him at a
risk for:
explanation:
Inherited homozygous protein C deficiency is a severe condition that is associated with
fetal central nervous system and retinal thrombotic events as well as neonatal purpura
fulminans. In contrast, heterozygous protein C deficiency puts a patient at moderate risk for
venous thromboembolism (VTE).
[QCMLS 2021: 5.7.2.2) [Kottke-Marchant 2016, p133)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 58 · boc2 PDF page 43

question: Protein S forms a reversible complex with:
explanation:
Protein S is carried through the circulation by C4b binding protein (C4bBP). An elevation
in C4bBP occurs in response to inflammatory conditions. When C4bBP is elevated, there
is an increase in the amount of bound protein S with a concomitant decrease in free and
functional protein S levels.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.6.2.3] [Kottke-Marchant 2016, p 303)

There is an unusually high prevalence of factor XI deficiency in Ashkenazi Jews.

question: Unregulated and excessive formation of thrombin and plasmin is seen in:
explanation:
In DIC, there is a generalized activation of hemostasis as a result of a systemic disease.
Circulating thrombin activates platelets and coagulation proteins and catalyzes fibrin
formation. As a result, the fibrinolytic system, at the level of plasminogen, becomes activated
leading to the presence of soluble fibrin monomers, fibrin polymer, and cross-linked fibrin in
the plasma, all of which serve to further activate plasminogen to plasmin. As platelets become
enmeshed in the fibrin polymer or are exposed to thrombin, platelet activation continues,
which continues to drive the coagulation system. At the same time protein C, protein S,
and antithrombin are consumed, resulting in a loss of control in the coagulation system.
The hemorrhagic picture in DIC is a result of thrombin activation, circulating plasmin, loss of
control, and thrombocytopenia.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.6.2.3] [Rodak 2020, p667]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 61 · boc2 PDF page 44

question:
A patient presents with a factor VIII level of 2%. The vWF activity (ristocetin cofactor) is <1 %
with a vWF antigen of 3%. The most likely diagnosis is:
explanation:
Type Ill von Willebrand disease is a rare, autosomal recessive disorder in which all vWF
multimers are absent or nearly absent from plasma. Factor VIII is proportionately diminished
or absent and so primary and secondary hemostasis is impaired. Type II vWD is comprised
of several qualitative abnormalities. Hemophilia A is a deficiency of FVIII with normal vWF
activity and antigen. Hemophilia B is a deficiency of factor IX.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.5.2.3.1, 15.7) [Rodak 2020, p660-661]

explanation:
In DIC the PT and aPTT are prolonged, the fibrinogen is decreased and the D-dimer in

[QCMLS 2021: 5.6.2.3.1] [Rodak 2020, p735]

and dietary deficiencies such as vitamin K deficiency may all be associated with bleeding.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.6.2.4] [Rodak 2020, p654-655]

Average life span of platelets in peripheral blood is 9.5 days.

question: Aspirin affects platelet function by interfering with platelet metabolism of:
explanation:
Aspirin interferes with prostaglandin metabolism in the platelet by inhibiting cyclooxygenase,
which participates in the conversion of arachidonic acid to protein G2; protein G2 is necessary
to produce thromboxane, which stimulates secretion from the platelet granules.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.5.2.2] [Rodak 2020, p684)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 69 · boc2 PDF page 45

question:
In patients who present with bleeding disorders caused by platelets, the most common type of
bleeding is:
explanation:
Certain characteristics of platelet-type bleeding disorders include mucosal bleeding,
petechiae, and a female predominance. Other types of bleeding are due to defects in
coagulation factors. Hemarthrosis and deep hematomas occur in factor VIII deficiency
(hemophilia), delayed bleeding occurs in factor XIII deficiency, and deep hematomas presents
with the other choices in the question.
(QCMLS 2021: 5.5] [Rodak 2020, p650-651]

question: The anticoagulant that is best directed against platelets is:
explanation:
Hirudin, argatroban and dabigatran are direct thrombin inhibitors. They are either isolated
from the leech, Hirudo medicinalis (hirudin ), or are recombinant forms of the same protein
(lepirudin, argatroban, dabigatran). Tirofiban is not related and is a platelet GPllb/llla inhibitor
and is an anti-platelet drug.
[QCMLS 2021 : 5.7.5.2.4]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 71 · boc2 PDF page 46

question: How do ticlopidine and clopidogrel inhibit platelets?
options: depletion of platelet alpha granule content
explanation:
Ticlopidine and clopidogrel both inhibit ADP mediated aggregation and present with
blunted ADP response with aggregometry studies, but normal results with other agonists.
Another class of inhibitors, like abciximab, block platelet function through GPllb/llla.
[QCMLS 2021 : 5.7.5.2.4] [Rodak 2020, p757-758]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 72 · boc2 PDF page 46

question: von Willebrand factor mediates platelet adhesion by binding to platelet receptor:
explanation:
vWF binds platelets through their GP lb/lXN membrane receptor. The importance of
platelet adhesion is demonstrated by bleeding disorders such as von Willebrand disease,
in which vWF is missing or defective, and Bernard-Soulier disease, in which the GP lb/lXN
receptor is absent.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.3.3, 15.1] [Rodak 2020, p658]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 73 · boc2 PDF page 46

question: The disease state that presents with a quantitative platelet disorder is:
explanation:
May-Hegglin anomaly is characterized by decreased platelet counts; vWD and hemophilia
patients do not present with low platelet counts. Glanzmann patients present with normal
platelet counts that do not function.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.5.2] [Rodak 2020, p678, 696]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 74 · boc2 PDF page 46

question:
A patient presents with a very low platelet count and is diagnosed with acute idiopathic
thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP). Which statement is associated with acute ITP?
options: it is found primarily in adults
spontaneous remission usually occurs within several weeks
peripheral destruction of platelets is decreased
explanation:

question: The most common cause of bleeding in patients is:
explanation:
A quantitative abnormality of platelets (thrombocytopenia) is the most common cause of
excessive or abnormal bleeding. Fibrinogen deficiencies are rare.
(QCMLS 2021 : 5.5) [Rodak 2020, p696]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 76 · boc2 PDF page 46

question: ADAMTS13 deficiency is responsible for thrombocytopenia found in:
explanation:
Patients with thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP} present with platelet counts
<20 x 103/µL ( <20 x 109/L). Platelet thrombi are dispersed throughout the arterioles and
capillaries subsequent to the accumulation of large vWF multimers made by endothelial cells
and platelets. This is related to a deficiency of ADAMTS-13. DIC is caused by inflammation,
infections and cancer. HUS is related to a toxin producing organism. ITP is a result of

question:
Heparin induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) is an immune mediated complication associated
with heparin therapy. Antibodies are produced against:
explanation:
The pathogenesis of HIT is that antibodies are produced against heparin- platelet factor 4
complex. This complex binds to FC receptors causing platelet activation and the formation of
platelet microparticles, thrombocytopenia and hypercoagulability. ACLA and B2GP1 are seen
in anti-phospholipid syndrome.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.7.4] [Rodak 2020, p737, 724]

question: In polycythemia vera, the platelet count is:

count are characteristic of Bernard-Soulier.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.5.1) (Rodak 2020, p678-679]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 83 · boc2 PDF page 47

question:
A patient with multimer pattern that has all bands present but in decreased concentrations
would be diagnosed with:
explanation:
In type 1 von Willebrand disease (vWD) the plasma concentration of all vWF multimers
and FVIII are variable, although proportionally reduced. Hemophilia presents with a normal
multimer pattern. Type 3 vWD has absent or greatly reduced multimers, with type 2 will have
varying multimer patterns based on the subtype.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.5.2.3.1, 15.7] [Rodak 2020, p659]

question:
Which characteristic of Bernard-Soulier syndrome helps distinguish it from von Willebrand
disease?
options: concomitant storage pool defects in platelets
explanation:
The platelets seen in the peripheral smear of patients with Bernard-Soulier syndrome
are typically larger than normal. Thrombocytopenia is usually present, yet is nonspecific.
Otherwise, the clinical presentation of von Willebrand disease (especially platelet-type, and
types 2M and 3) and Bernard-Soulier are strikingly similar.
(QCMLS 2021: 5.5.1.1) [Rodak 2020, p661, 678-679]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 85 · boc2 PDF page 48

question:
Which of the following characteristics are common between Hermansky-Pudlak and
Chediak-Higashi syndromes?
explanation:
Both Hermansky-Pudlak and Chediak-Higashi are due to defects in dense granule
storage, where platelets store small molecules in order to initiate the secondary wave of
aggregation. Inclusion granules are more common in Chediak-Higashi, while ceroidlike
inclusions are more common in Hermansky-Pudlak. Alpha granule defects are not usually
seen in either.
(QCMLS 2021: 5.5.2.1] [Rodak 2020, p681]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 86 · boc2 PDF page 48

question: Patients with Wiscott-Aldrich syndrome present with:
explanation:
A similar syndrome of thrombocytopenia with absent radii is most commonly seen in
patient without radii and thumbs. Wiskott-Aldrich also presents with platelet-type bleeding, like
Hermansky-Pudlak and Chediak-Higashi.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.5.1.1] [Rodak 2020, p681-682]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 87 · boc2 PDF page 48

question:
When evaluating a patient for von Willebrand disorder, the ABO blood type that has the lowest
level of vWF is:
explanation:
The choices are organized in order of the relative amount of von Willebrand factor.
There can be an almost 50% difference in the amount of vWF between type O and types B
or AB. The lower reference range for vWF for type O is 35% vs 64% in type AB.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.5.2.3.3) [Rodak 2020, p662]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 88 · boc2 PDF page 48

question:
Which subtype of von Willebrand disease is the most common?
MlS
explanation:
By far the majority of cases of von Willebrand disease (vWD) are type 1, up to 75%
of patients. Type 1 is due to decreased levels of von Willebrand factor (vWF). Type 3 is
an absence of vWF and is found in less than 5% of vWD patients, while type 2 (and its
subclasses) are due to functional defects in vWF and makes up between 7-30% of vWD
cases.
(QCMLS 2021: 5.5.2.3.1.1] [Rodak 2020, p659-660]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 89 · boc2 PDF page 48

question: Which of the following types of von Willebrand disease should not be treated with DDAVP?
explanation:
DDAVP stimulates the release of vWF and FVIII from Weibel-Palade bodies. Type 2B
vWD reacts to DDAVP with enhanced platelet aggregation leading to potentially dangerous
thrombosis, while type 3 does not react at all.
[QCMLS 2021 : 5.5.2.3.1.1] [Rodak 2020, p663]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 90 · boc2 PDF page 48

question: TTP presents with a pentad of symptoms that does not include:
explanation:
The classic pentad of symptoms for TTP can be remembered with the insensitive "FAT
RN" mnemonic: Fever, anemia, thrombocytopenia, renal failure, neurological symptoms.
Clinically TTP can overlap with HUS.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.5.1.2.2, !5.5] [Rodak 2020, p365]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 91 · boc2 PDF page 48

question:
A 40-year-old female has pinpoint hemorrhages on her legs, with an Hct of 43% and a platelet
count of 19 x 103/µL (19 x 109/L). Steroids fail to increase platelet count. The patient's
diagnosis is:
explanation:
Most cases of chronic immune thrombocytopenic purpura occur in patients between
the ages of 20 and 50 years. Females with the disorder generally outnumber males.
Presenting features include petechiae and ecchymoses.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.5.1.2.1] [Rodak 2020, p702]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 92 · boc2 PDF page 49

question:
A 60-year-old female presents with blurred vision, confusion, and petechiae with a platelet
count of 29 x 103/µL (29 x 109/L).
test
result
PT
12.1 seconds (11.4-13.5 seconds))
aPTT
32.6 seconds (25-35 seconds)
The CBC RBC morphology shows schistocytes. The differential diagnosis should include:
explanation:
TTP is characterized by the triad of macroangiopathic hemolytic anemia,
thrombocytopenia, and neurologic abnormalities. In addition, fever and renal dysfunction
(forming a pentad) are often present. The PT and aPTT, are usually normal and may be useful
in differentiating this disorder from DIC.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.5.1.2.2] [Rodak 2020, p707-708]

question: One of the main difference between TTP and HUS is:
explanation:
The lack of neurologic symptoms, the presence of renal dysfunction, and the absence of
other organ involvement suggest HUS.
(QCMLS 2021: 5.5.1.2.2, 15.5) [Rodak 2020, p710]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 94 · boc2 PDF page 49

question:
Several hours after birth an infant develops petechiae, purpuric hemorrhages and a platelet
count of 21 x 103/µL (21 x 109/L). The most likely diagnosis is:
explanation:
The causes of neonatal thrombocytopenia are numerous and present at or within
72 hours of birth.
(QCMLS 2021: 5.5.1.2.2) [Rodak 2020, p705]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 95 · boc2 PDF page 49

question: In TTP, a deficiency of ADAMTS13 causes clotting because of:
options: inability to produce antibodies to prevent platelet aggregation
explanation:
In TTP, inherited or acquired defective ADAMTS13 enzyme activity is associated with
the presence of ultra-large vWF multimers in plasma resulting in platelet aggregations and
microvascular thrombosis.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.5.1.2.2) [Rodak 2020, p708]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 96 · boc2 PDF page 49

question:
An orthopedic patient who is on heparin has a platelet count of 50 x 103/µL (50 x 109/L); his
platelet count the previous day was 120 x 103/µL (120 x 109/L). The patient is tested for HIT
and has a positive result. The first step in the treatment of HIT is:
explanation:
HIT is a relatively common side effect of unfractionated heparin administration with
about 1-5% of patients developing this complication. In patients who develop HIT heparin
should be stopped as soon as the diagnosis is made. It is not recommended to switch to
LMWH or warfarin, and giving a patient platelets will cause clotting since platelets are already
aggregating in vivo. Patients are treated with antithrombins.
[QCMLS 2021 : 5.7.4] [Rodak 2020, p737)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 97 · boc2 PDF page 49

question: In HELLP syndrome patients present with:
explanation:
HELLP syndrome affects an estimated 4-12% of pregnant women with severe preeclampsia (hypertension). It is named for its characteristic presentation of hemolysis, elevated
liver enzymes, and low platelet count.
[QCMLS 2021 : 5.5.2.2) [Rodak 2020, p367)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 98 · boc2 PDF page 49

question:
von Willebrand factor serves as a stabilizer for:
f.lLS
explanation:
von Willebrand factor (vWF) functions as a protective carrier protein for factor VIII, thus
participating in the formation of the fibrin clot. FVlll levels may be decreased in von Willebrand
disease because the half-life of FVIII shortens when it is not bound to vWF.
(QCMLS 2021: 5.5.2.3) [Kottke-Marchant 2016, p241)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 99 · boc2 PDF page 50

question: The platelet disorder in which the abnormality is due to a defect in platelet aggregation is:
explanation:
Glanzmann thrombasthenia is a disorder of platelet aggregation in which there is a
deficiency or abnormality of the platelet membrane glycoprotein GP lib/Illa, a receptor that is
capable of binding fibrinogen and von Willebrand factor. In contrast, von Willebrand disease
and Bernard-Soulier syndrome are both disorders of platelet adhesion and storage pool
diseases are disorders of platelet secretion.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.5.2.1, 15.6) [Rodak 2020, p677]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 100 · boc2 PDF page 50

question: Large blue inclusions bodies in WBC are found in patients with:
explanation:
May-Hegglin anomaly is a rare, autosomal dominant platelet disorder. Patients present
with variable thrombocytopenia, giant platelets, and large Dohle body-like inclusions
in the neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils, and monocytes. The majority of patients are
asymptomatic, but a few have shown mild bleeding tendencies related to the degree of
thrombocytopenia. Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome and Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome are both
disorders of platelet secretion, specifically storage pool disorders. Ehlers-Danlos syndrome
is a vascular disorder in which a bleeding tendency is manifested primarily in subcutaneous
hematoma formation.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.8.2)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 101 · boc2 PDF page 50

question:
An initial prenatal evaluation at 10 weeks is conducted on a healthy female. PT, aPTT
and fibrinogen are normal with the exception of her platelet count, which is 42,000/ml.
The peripheral smear shows platelet clumps. What is the next step?
options: conduct a workup for an autoimmune disease
recollect the sample in sodium citrate
explanation:
Low platelet counts can be caused by EDTA-dependent platelet agglutinins and occur in
healthy people, they are not known to be associated with any pathological condition. There is
no risk to the patient for thromboembolism or autoimmune disease. Recollecting the sample
in sodium citrate should normalize the platelet count.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.5)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 102 · boc2 PDF page 50

question: The initial platelet adhesion to subendothelial matrix proteins is abnormal in:
options: von Willebrand disease and Bernard-Soulier syndrome
explanation:
In Bernard-Soulier the abnormality is on the platelet receptor for vWF, and in vWD
is it in the structure of vWF resulting in an abnormality in the initial platelet adhesion to
subendothelium. GP lib/Illa inhibitors effect the formation of platelet aggregation. Patients
with hemophilia A or B have abnormality of thrombin generation and do not have any platelet
abnormality, nor do patients with factor XIII deficiency. They present with delayed bleeding
due to a decreased level of fibrin stabilizing factor.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.5.2.1]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 103 · boc2 PDF page 50

question:
A 2-year-old child presents with recurrent epistaxis, gum bleeding and occasional hematuria,
upon physical exam showed petechiae and ecchymoses. The patient is not on any
medication. PT and aPTT and platelet count are normal. Platelet function screen tests are
abnormal, and a platelet aggregation test is ordered. Results are:
absent aggregation with ADP, collagen, epinephrine
ristocetin inducted platelet aggregation: within reference range
The differential diagnosis should include:
explanation:
Glanzmann thrombasthenia is characterized by an absent aggregation to all agonists,
the normal ristocetin induced platelet aggregation distinguishes it from Bernard-Soulier. This
would also be abnormal in von Willebrand disorder.
[QCMLS 2021 : 5.5.2)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 104 · boc2 PDF page 50

question: Quantitative platelet disorders can be due to:
explanation:
Platelets can be decreased in number based on any of the disorders. A qualitative
disorder of platelets can be caused by abnormal structure or function of platelets.
[QCMLS 2021 : 5.5.1)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 105 · boc2 PDF page 50

question: Post-transfusion purpura is a rare form of:
explanation:
Post-transfusion purpura results in severe thrombocytopenia 3-12 days after a blood
transfusion, in which platelet destruction is caused by antibodies produced against platelet
antigen PLA-1a (HPA-1a).
[QCMLS 2021: 5.5.1.3.2)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 106 · boc2 PDF page 50

question: Disorders of platelet aggregation are found in:
explanation:
vWD and Bernard-Soulier are disorders of adhesion, while storage pool deficiency is an
abnormality of platelet granules.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.5.2)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 107 · boc2 PDF page 51

question: Spontaneous bleeding occurs when the platelet count is:
explanation:
A spontaneous bleed is seen in patients with counts <20 x 103/µL, while a life-threatening
bleed may be seen at <10 x 1O3/µL. Clinical symptoms do not usually appear until counts are
<100 x 1O3/µL, but are more likely at <50 x 103/µL.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.5.1)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 108 · boc2 PDF page 51

question: In hemolytic uremic syndrome, patients present with:
explanation:
Acute renal failure is a frequent presenting symptom of HUS. Severe CNS symptoms and
fever occur in patients with TTP.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.5.2.1)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 109 · boc2 PDF page 51

question:
A 65-year-old male has a valve replacement, and 5 days postoperatively his platelet count
had fallen to 80,000 after an initial count of 320,000. Also noted is swelling of his right calf.
The following day the platelet count is 30,000. What should be investigated, and what
therapeutic step is appropriate?
explanation:
The treatment for patients with HIT is to first stop heparin, and a direct thrombin
inhibitor should be administered. LMWH should not be administered because it can cause
cross-reactivity and platelet aggregation. Neither platelets nor plasma are indicated and would
be more harmful to the patient.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.7.4)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 110 · boc2 PDF page 51

question: In renal dysfunction uremia can cause:
explanation:
In acute and chronic renal diseases, often a bleeding tendency is associated with several
hemostatic abnormalities. Thrombocytopenia frequently develops in uremia.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.6.2.5)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 111 · boc2 PDF page 51

question:
A 70-year-old female with metastatic ovarian carcinoma shows elevated PT and aPTT,
platelets 15,000/mm3 and an elevated D-dimer. The differential diagnosis should include:
explanation:
The patient has all of the characteristics of a patient with disseminated intravascular
coagulation (DIC), which is a consumptive coagulopathy and occurs in many patients with
cancer. HUS occurs in children and TTP presents with neurological symptoms and organ
involvement.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.6.2.3)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 112 · boc2 PDF page 51

question:
A patient presents with a platelet count of 223 x 109/L with an abnormal PFA most possibly
suggest:
explanation:
The platelet count for this patient is normal, however when screen the functionality of the
platelets the result is abnormal suggesting defective platelet function.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.8.1.1)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 113 · boc2 PDF page 51

question: Which of the following is not an inherited vascular defect?
explanation:
May-Hegglin disorder is a rare inherited blood platelet disorder characterized by
abnormally large platelets and WBC defects. All of the rest are inherited vascular disorders.
[QCMLS 2021 : 5.2.2.1)
Ill. Laboratory Determinations
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 114 · boc2 PDF page 51

question:
A patient is placed on clopidogrel. The clinician wants to determine if the dose is sufficient to
impair platelet function. A platelet aggregation test is ordered. The agonist which would result
in a decreased aggregation pattern would be:
explanation:
Clopidogrel is a member of the thienopyridine drug family which occupy the platelet
membrane adenosine disphosphate (ADP) P2Y12. As a result, you would expect a
suppressed platelet aggregation response to ADP.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.7.5.2.2) [Rodak 2020, p685, 774]

question:
A platelet aggregation tracing appears to confirm the diagnosis of Glanzmann thrombasthenia
in a patient presenting with a platelet disorder. How would these tracings look if they were
performed using light transmittance optical density aggregation?
options: markedly decreased aggregation to epinephrine, ADP and collagen
explanation:
Glanzmann thrombasthenia is characterized by abnormal aggregation to ADP,
epinephrine and collagen, and normal aggregation to ristocetin.
[QCMLS 2021: 5:5.2] [Kottke-Marchant 2016, p217)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 116 · boc2 PDF page 52

question:
A patient has been taking aspirin regularly for arthritic pain. Which one of the following tests is
most likely to be abnormal in this patient?
explanation:
The PFA-100 assesses platelet function and is abnormal in the presence of aspirin.
The platelet count only assesses platelet number. The PT and aPTT cannot be used to
assess platelet number or function.
[QCMLS 2021 : 5.7.5.2.1) [Kottke-Marchant 2016, p104-106)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 117 · boc2 PDF page 52

question:
Which of the following platelet responses is most likely associated with type lib von Willebrand
disease?
MLs
options: decreased platelet aggregation to low-dose ristocetin
normal platelet aggregation to low-dose ristocetin
explanation:
vWD is characterized by abnormal platelet aggregation to ristocetin and normal platelet
aggregation to epinephrine, ADP and collagen. In type llb vWD, as well as in platelet-type
vWD, the response to low-dose ristocetin is increased, whereas in all other forms of vWD the
ristocetin response is decreased or normal.
[QCMLS 2021 : 5.5.2.3.1.2] [Kottke-Marchant 2016, p243-247]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 118 · boc2 PDF page 52

question: Platelet aggregation will occur with the end production of:
explanation:
Thromboxane A2 is necessary for normal platelet aggregation. Its formation initiates a
series of events, which results in the secretion and aggregation of platelets.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.8.1.3]

explanation:
Glanzmann thrombasthenia is an autosomal recessive disorder. Patients will have a
prolonged bleeding time and PFA-100, normal platelet count and morphology, and abnormal
aggregation with all aggregating agents except ristocetin.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.5.1.2] [Kottke-Marchant 2016, p214-217)

question: Which of the following will not affect the PFA-100 closure time?
explanation:
The PFA-100 assay measures platelet function by exposing a blood sample to high shear
forces and causing the platelets to aggregate, thereby simulating platelet plug formation.
The time for the aperture to close is directly proportional to platelet function. Aspirin interferes
with platelet function and will cause an abnormal PFA. However, not only do platelet function
disorders interfere with the PFA-100 closure times but thrombocytopenic and anemic samples
can also give artifactually lengthened closure times.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.8.1.1] [Kottke-Marchant 2016, p104-106]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 121 · boc2 PDF page 53

question:
What does the secondary wave of platelet aggregation seen with the biphasic low-dose ADP
and epinephrine response represent?
explanation:
Platelet-dense granules store molecules such as ATP, Ca2+, and serotonin, which cause
recruitment of additional platelets when released leading to further stimulation of platelet
aggregation. Initial stimulation (primary wave) is due to the direct action of low-dose ADP or
low-dose epinephrine on the GPllb/llla platelet membrane receptor.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.8.1.3.1] [Kottke-Marchant 2016, p18, 107)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 122 · boc2 PDF page 53

question:
Which of the following tests provides an appropriate laboratory confirmation of immune
~Y mediated heparin induced thrombocytopenia (type 2)?
explanation:
While the assay for anti-PF4 antibody is the most commonly performed confirmatory test,
it is less specific than either the gold standard serotonin release assay or the heparin induced
platelet aggregation assay.
{QCMLS 2021: 5.7.4)

question: The principle of platelet aggregation is based on:
explanation:
The optical turbidimetric platelet aggregation assay measures the increase in light
transmission that occurs in direct proportion to platelet aggregation when various agonists
such as ADP, collagen, epinephrine, arachidonic acid, and ristocetin are used to induce
platelet aggregation. The test sample is platelet-rich plasma. As aggregation proceeds, there
is a gradual clearing of the plasma as platelet aggregates form. This clearing results in an
increase in light transmission measured spectrophotometrically and tracings of the reactions
are displayed on a graph.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.8.1.3.1] [Rodak 2020, p771-772]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 124 · boc2 PDF page 53

Whole blood evaluation of blood clotting can be performed by using thromboelastography.
This methodology looks at:
MLs
explanation:
Thromboelastography tracings can detect and report clot onset, clot strength, and
fibrinolysis within 15 minutes of blood collection.
[QCMLS 2021 : 5.8.1.4) [Rodak 2020, p803]

The tracing in this figure is from a cardiac surgery patient using thromboelastography.
This tracing shows the patient during cardiac surgery is:

explanation:
This is a global whole-blood analyzer that measures clotting time and dynamics,
clot strength, antithrombotic effects, platelet effects on clot dynamics and strength, and
fibrinolysis. It is used mainly in liver and cardiac surgeries. Analysis of the tracing determine
the speed, strength, and stability of clot formation as well as the effect of fibrinolysis.
[QCMLS 2021 : 5.8.1.4) [Rodak 2020, p803]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 127 · boc2 PDF page 54

question:
A patient sample has been tested in the routine laboratory with a PT and an aPTT. Six hours
later factor assays are ordered on the same sample. Which factor is the most labile?
explanation:
Factors V and VIII are considered labile factors because their activity diminishes quickly
at room temperature.
[QCMLS 2021 : 5.4.1, 15.2] [Kottke-Marchant 2016, p48]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 128 · boc2 PDF page 54

question:
A patient presents with an aPTT of 62.5 seconds (25-35 seconds) and the only factor that is
decreased is factor XII. What is the clinical picture for this patient?
explanation:
Patients with a deficiency of factor XII tend to have thrombotic complications. They do
not have bleeding problems, most likely due to the lack of activation of fibrin lysis as well as
the lack of both the activation of factor IX by the factor VI la/TF complex and the activation of
factor XI by thrombin.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.6.1.2) [Rodak 2020, p636]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 129 · boc2 PDF page 54
