question: A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus that is bacitracin-sensitive and CAMP-negative is:
options: beta-hemolytic, not group A, 8, or D
explanation:
Group A streptococci (Streptococcus pyogenes) are susceptible to bacitracin and
CAMP-test-negative.
[QCMLS 2021: 6.1.6.1.2.1) [Procop 2017, p788J
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 162 · boc2 PDF page 115

question:
The organism seen in the image below is bacitracin-resistant and CAMP-positive. The
identification is:
explanation:
Streptococcus agalactiae is beta-hemolytic, resistant to bacitracin and CAMP test
positive.
[QCMLS 2021 : 6.1.6.1.2.1] [Procop 2017, p788]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 163 · boc2 PDF page 116

question: It is important to differentiate between Enterococcus and group D streptococci because:
options: viridans streptococci are often confused with enterococci
several enterococci cause severe puerperal sepsis
enterococci often show more antibiotic resistance than group D streptococci
explanation:
Enterococcus species are more resistant to antimicrobial therapy than group D
streptococci such as S. bovis.
[QCMLS 2021: 6.1.6.1.2.3] [Procop 2017, p767]

Streptococcus pneumoniae can be differentiated best from the viridans group of streptococci
by:

Bile solubility testing of alpha-hemolytic streptococci differentiates S. pneumoniae

question: Characteristically, enterococci are:
explanation:
Enterococci are bile-esculin-positive, hippurate-negative and have the ability to grow in
6.5% NaCl. Enterococci are relatively resistant to penicillin and require combination therapy to
treat serious infections.
[QCMLS 2021: 6.1.6.1.2.3) [Procop 2017, 773, 788]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 167 · boc2 PDF page 116

question:
Which of the following would best differentiate Streptococcus aga/actiae from
Streptococcus pyogenes?
options: ability to grow in sodium azide broth
explanation:
Of the biochemicals listed, only hydrolysis of sodium hippurate will differentiate
Streptococcus agalactiae (positive) from S. pyogenes (negative).
[QCMLS 2021: 6.1.6.1.2.1) [Procop 2017, p788]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 168 · boc2 PDF page 116

question: Members of the family Enterobacteriaceae share which one of the following characteristics?
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 177 · boc2 PDF page 118

question:
Which one of these genera is among the least biochemically reactive members of the
Enterobacteriaceae?
explanation:
Shigella is lactose-negative, most species do not produce gas, are VP, urea, lysine
decarboxylase and citrate-negative, and they are nonmotile.
[QCMLS 2021: 6.1.6.4.1) [Procop 2017, p250]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 178 · boc2 PDF page 118

question: Which one of these gram-negative bacilli ferments glucose?
explanation:
Alcaligenes, Pseudomonas and Acinetobacter are all nonfermenters; Yersinia is a
member of the Enterobacteriaceae and, by definition, ferments glucose.
[QCMLS 2021: 6.1.6.4.1) [Procop 2017, p250)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 179 · boc2 PDF page 118

question:
P/esiomonas shigelloides is a member of the family Enterobacteriaceae. The characteristic
that differentiates Pleisiomonas from other Enterobacteriaeae is:
explanation:
Enterobacteriaceae ferment glucose and are oxidase-negative. Plesiomonas was a
member of the Vibrio family in part because it is oxidase-positive. However, it was moved to
the Enterobacteriaceae family despite its positive oxidase reaction.
[QCMLS 2021: 6.1.6.4.2) [Procop 2017, p461)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 183 · boc2 PDF page 119

question:
An organism that exhibits the satellite phenomenon around colonies of Staphylococcus
aureus is:
explanation:
Haemophilus influenzae requires X (hemin) and V (NAO) factors. Sheep blood agar
streaked with Staphylococcus aureus supplies X factor, and V factor, so colonies grow around
the S. aureus colonies.
[QCMLS 2021 : 6.1.6.4.4) [Procop 2017, p484]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 189 · boc2 PDF page 120

question: Acinetobacter lwoffii differs from Neisseria gonorrhoeae in that Acinetobacter.
options:
exhibits a gram-negative staining reaction
MlS
will grow on MacConkey and EMB media
produces hydrogen sulfide on a TSI slant
explanation:
Both organisms are gram-negative. Neisseria gonorrhoeae is fastidious and does not
grow on MacConkey or EMB agar, but Acinetobacter does. Neisseria is oxidase-positive and
Acinetobacter is oxidase-negative.
[QCMLS 2021 : 6.1.6.4.3) [Procop 2017, p373, 382)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 190 · boc2 PDF page 120

question:
A characteristic that is helpful in separating Pseudomonas aeruginosa from other members of
the Pseudomonas family is:
options: a positive test for cytochrome oxidase
oxidative metabolism in the OF test
explanation:
Pseudomonas aeruginosa grows at 42°C, but this temperature is inhibitory for other
Pseudomonas species.
[QCMLS 2021: 6.1.6.4.3) (Tille 2016, p341]
~

source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 191 · boc2 PDF page 120

question: Which characteristic best differentiates Acinetobacter species from Moraxella species?
explanation:
Both Acinetobacter and Moraxella display resistance to penicillin, Acinetobacter
grows on MacConkey agar and some species of Moraxella can grow on MacConkey agar
(M. os/oensis and M. nonliquefaciens.) Acinetobacter are oxidase-negative, and Moraxel/a
are oxidase-positive.
[QCMLS 2021: 6.1.6.4.3] [Procop 2017, p381-382]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 194 · boc2 PDF page 121

question:
Characteristics of the genus Capnocytophaga include:
1.11.S
options: colonies are large and spreading after 2-4 days
explanation:
Capnocytophaga require CO2 environment, ferment glucose, sucrose, and lactose, and
are gram-negative bacilli. Capnocytophaga produce characteristic spreading colonies with
finger-like projections.
[QCMLS 2021: 6.1.6.4.3] [Procop 2017, p499)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 196 · boc2 PDF page 121

question:
Characteristics of the HACEK group of bacteria include:
MlS
options: Gram stain of pleomorphic gram-positive bacilli
explanation:
The HACEK group of organisms are gram-negative bacilli that require increased CO2 for
growth. They are commonly associated with endocarditis, and include Haemophilus species
(especially H. aphrophilus), Aggregatibacter (formerly Actinobacillus) actinomycetemcomitans,
Cardiobacterium hominis, Eikenella corrodens, and Kingella species.
[QCMLS 2021: 6.1.6.4.4) [lille 2016, p874)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 198 · boc2 PDF page 121

question: Which genera are positive for phenylalanine deaminase (PAD) production?
explanation:
There are key reactions for Enterobacteriaceae that are important to remember.
Phenylalanine deaminase is a biochemical that is helpful in initialing differentiation Proteus,
Providencia, and Morganella from other Enterobacteriaceae.
[QCMLS 2021: 6.1.6.4.1] [Procop 2017, p235]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 200 · boc2 PDF page 122

question: All species of the genus Neisseria have the enzyme to oxidize:
explanation:
Since all Neisseria species are oxidase-positive, they possess the enzyme to oxidize
tetramethyl-phenylenediamine.
[QCMLS 2021: 6.1.6.2) [Mahon 2019, p183, 372)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 202 · boc2 PDF page 122

question: A method for the definitive identification of Neisseria gonorrhoeae is:
explanation:
Of the choices provided, only utilization of carbohydrates provides definitive identification
of Neisseria gonorrhoeae.
[QCMLS 2021 : 6.1.6.2) [Mahon 2019, p375]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 204 · boc2 PDF page 122

question:
Which feature distinguishes Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae from other clinically significant
non-spore-forming, gram-positive, facultatively anaerobic bacilli?
explanation:
Erysipelothrix rhusopathiae are the only gram-positive bacilli that produce hydrogen
sulfide when inoculated into triple sugar iron agar.
[QCMLS 2021 : 6.1.6.3) [Mahon 2019, p354-355)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 209 · boc2 PDF page 123

question: Listeria can be confused with some Streptococcaceae because it is beta-hemolytic and:
explanation:
Listeria may be confused with some streptococci because Listeria is beta-hemolytic and is
capable of hydrolyzing esculin.
[QCMLS 2021 : 6.1.6.3] [Mahon 2019, p355]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 210 · boc2 PDF page 123

question:
The reverse CAMP test, lecithinase production, double zone hemolysis, and Gram stain
morphology are all useful criteria in the identification of:
explanation:
Production of lecithinase and demonstration of double zone hemolysis are tests and
characteristics used for the identification of Clostridium perfringens.
[QCMLS 2021 : 6.1.6.5.4] [Mahon 2019, p506-507]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 213 · boc2 PDF page 124

question: Which of the following sets of organisms may exhibit a brick red fluorescence?
explanation:
Prevotella and Porphyromonas (as well as Veil/one/la parvu/a) produce colonies that
fluoresce brick red.
[QCMLS 2021: 6.1.6.5.6] [Mahon 2019, p506-507)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 214 · boc2 PDF page 124

question: Penicillin resistance in Neisseria gonorrhoeae can be due to the organism producing:
explanation:
Antimicrobial resistance in Neisseria gonorrhoeae is widespread. One mechanism of
penicillin resistance is the production of beta-lactamase (penicillinase) that breaks open the
beta lactam ring of penicillin, destroying its activity. Thus, N. gonorrhoeae that produce beta
lactamase are resistant to penicillin. Detection of the other listed enzymes can be used to
identify other gram-negative diplococci.
(QCMLS 2021: 6.3.3) [Mahon 2019, p282-283]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 220 · boc2 PDF page 125

question: The most sensitive substrate for the detection of beta-lactamases is:
explanation:
The chromogenic cephalosporin test using nitrocefin is the most sensitive and specific
test for detection of beta-lactamase. Acidimetric tests employing penicillin are less expensive,
but not as sensitive, as the nitrocefin assay.
[QCMLS 2021: 6.3.3] [Procop 2017, p1119]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 221 · boc2 PDF page 125

question: An antibiotic that inhibits cell wall synthesis is:
explanation:
Penicillin inhibits penicillin binding proteins that are essential to peptidoglycan (cell wall)
synthesis. Penicillin is a beta-lactam antibiotic. All beta-lactam antibiotics inhibit cell wall
synthesis. Chloramphenicol inhibits protein synthesis, colistin increases cell membrane
permeability, and sulfamethoxazole inhibits folate metabolism.
[QCMLS 2021: 6.3.1] [Mahon 2019, p250-251]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 229 · boc2 PDF page 126

question:
When using a control strain of Staphylococcus aureus, the technologist notices that the zone
around the cefoxitin disk is too small. Which of the following is the most likely explanation?
options: inoculation of the plates 10 minutes after preparing the inoculum
incubation of the Mueller-Hinton plates at 35°C
use of a 0.25 McFarland standard to prepare inoculum
explanation:
Deterioration of the antimicrobial agent in the disk will cause the zone sizes to be
too small (falsely resistant). Standardization of the inoculum turbidity to less than a
0.5 McFarland standard would result in an inoculum that is too light and resulting zone sizes
that are too large. Incubation of the plates at 35°C and inoculating plates within 1 0 minutes
of preparation would not have an adverse effect on zone sizes.
(QCMLS 2021: 6.3.3) [Procop 2017, p1108]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 232 · boc2 PDF page 127

question:
A Klebsiella pneumoniae isolate is known to produce carbapenemase;
therefore, it therapeutically will not respond to the antibiotics:
explanation:
Organisms producing carbapenemase are typically resistant to carbapenems
(eg, imipenem) and also penicillins (eg, amoxicillin), cephalosporins (eg, cefazolin),
fluoroquinolones (eg, ciprofloxacin), and sometimes aminoglycosides (eg, gentamicin).
[QCMLS 2021: 6.3.3] [Procop 2017, p270-271]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 239 · boc2 PDF page 128

question:
Representative beta-lactam antibiotics and their mechanism of action include:
Ml.S
options: ampicillin, cefazolin and imipenem; and inhibition of cell wall synthesis
ampicillin, cefazolin and imipenem; and inhibition of DNA replication
ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin and aztreonam; and inhibition of cell wall synthesis
ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin and aztreonam; and inhibition of DNA replication
explanation:
Beta-lactam antibiotics inhibit cell wall synthesis. Beta-lactam antibiotic examples include:
penicillins (eg, ampicillin), cephalosporins (eg, cefazolin), and carbapenems (eg, imipenem).
[QCMLS 2021: 6.3.1) [Mahon 2019, p250]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 240 · boc2 PDF page 129

question: Haemophilus influenzae becomes resistant to ampicillin when the organism produces:
explanation:
The beta-lactamase enzyme produced by Haemophilus influenzae inactivates
the antibiotics that have a beta-lactam ring in their structure, such as penicillins and
cephalosporins.
(QCMLS 2021: 6.3.3] [TIiie 2016, p407, 408]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 241 · boc2 PDF page 129

question: Clinical resistance to penicillin correlates most frequently with beta-lactamase production in:
explanation:
Neisseria meningitidis is rarely resistant to penicillin, which can be beta-lactamase
mediated in some isolates. The primary mechanism of penicillin resistance in N. gonorrhoeae
is beta-lactamase. Treponema pallidum is sensitive to penicillin, while treatment for
Chlamydia is doxycycline and azithromycin.
[QCMLS 2021: 6.3.3]
L. MRSAJMSSA, VRE, ESBUCRE Screening
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 242 · boc2 PDF page 129

question: Examples of Category A agents of bioterrorism include:
explanation:
Category A agents of bioterrorism potentially have the greatest impact on public health for
transmission, morbidity and mortality. Francisella tularensis and Yersinia pestis are Category
A, as well as Bacillus anthracis, and variola major virus (smallpox). MOR tuberculosis and
Hanta virus are Category C agents. VRE and Bacillus cereus are not considered agents of
bioterrorism.
[QCMLS 2021: 6.1.5) [Mahon 2019, p725, 727]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 244 · boc2 PDF page 129

question: BSL-3 organisms are those that:
options: cause human disease but are not readily transmitted among hosts
do not ordinarily cause human disease; they require minimal safety procedures
have very high risk of serious disease and no available treatment or vaccine
produce serious disease and are transmitted by respiratory route
explanation:
BSL-3 organisms produce serious disease and are transmitted by respiratory route.
BSL-2 organisms are not readily transmitted; BSL-1 organisms don't cause human disease;
BSL-4 organisms cause serious disease for which there is neither treatment nor vaccine.
[QCMLS 2021: 6.1.5] [Mahon 2019, p728]

question:
A branching gram-positive, partially acid-fast organism is isolated from a bronchial washing
on a 63-year-old woman receiving chemotherapy. The organism does not hydrolyze casein,
tyrosine or xanthine. The most likely genus causing the infection is:
explanation:
Nocardia asteroides are partially acid fast, and do not hydrolyze the substrates casein,
tyrosine, or xanthine. The most reliable method for ID is 16S rRNA gene sequencing.
[QCMLS 2021: 6.1.6.3] [Mahon 2019, p358-359]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 246 · boc2 PDF page 129

question: The disease-producing capacity of Mycobacterium tuberculosis depends primarily upon:
options: capacity to withstand intracellular digestion by macrophages

lack of susceptibility to the myeloperoxidase system
-~~---------'-'---~-----'---
explanation:
Mycobacterium tuberculosis can remain viable but dormant in macrophages for many
years.
(QCMLS 2021 : 6.2.1.5) [Mahon 2019, p256]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 260 · boc2 PDF page 131

question:
What Mycobacterium species includes a BCG strain used for vaccination against
tuberculosis?
explanation:
BCG strains of Mycobacterium bovis have been used as a vaccine in highly endemic
areas of the world.
[QCMLS 2021: 6.2.1.5) [Procop 2017, p1240]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 261 · boc2 PDF page 132

question: A primary drug used for the treatment of Mycobacterium tuberculosis is:
explanation:
Primary drugs for Mycobacterium tuberculosis treatment include isoniazid, rifampin,
pyrazinamide, streptomycin and ethambutol.
[QCMLS 2021: 6.2.1.5) [Mahon 2019, p558]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 263 · boc2 PDF page 132

question:
When grown in the dark, yellow-to-orange pigmentation of the colonies is usually
demonstrated by:
explanation:
Mycobacterium scrofu/aceum is a scotochromogen, which produces carotene pigment
when grown in the light or dark.
[QCMLS 2021: 6.2.1.5) [Mahon 2019, p560-561]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 264 · boc2 PDF page 132

question:
The mycobacteria that produce a deep yellow or orange pigment both in the dark and in
light are:
explanation:
Scotochromogens produce deep yellow or orange pigment when grown in either light or
darkness.
[QCMLS 2021: 6.2.1.5] [Mahon 2019, p559]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 265 · boc2 PDF page 132

question: Mycobacteria that produce pigment only after exposure to light are classified as:
explanation:
Photochromogens produce nonpigmented colonies only when grown in darkness, but
pigmented colonies after exposure to light.
(QCMLS 2021: 6.2.1.5) [Mahon 2019, p559]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 266 · boc2 PDF page 132

question: In a suspected case of Hansen disease (leprosy), a presumptive diagnosis is established by:
options: isolation of organisms on Lowenstein-Jensen medium
detection of weakly acid-fast bacilli in infected tissue
isolation of organisms in a cell culture
detection of niacin production by the isolated bacterium
explanation:
Mycobacterium leprae cannot be cultured in vitro. A clinical diagnosis is made, supported
by the presence of AFB in a biopsy specimen.
[QCMLS 2021: 6.2.1.7) [Mahon 2019, p652-563]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 267 · boc2 PDF page 132

question:
Differentiation of Mycobacterium avium from Mycobacterium intrace/lulare can be
~tv accomplished by:
options: resistance to 10 µg thiophene-2-carboxylic acid hydrazide (TCH)
explanation:
Mycobacterium avium and M. intracel/ulare have the same biochemical pattern, but can
be differentiated by the use of molecular diagnostic tests.
[QCMLS 2021 : 6.2.1.7) [Mahon 2019, p559]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 270 · boc2 PDF page 133

question:
Organisms that are part of the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (MTBC) include
Mycobacterium tuberculosis and:
explanation:
Mycobacterium tuberculosis, M. africanum, M. bovis and M. microti are genotypically
related and are considered members of the MTBC. These organisms can be differentiated by
phenotypic characteristics, including colony morphology, niacin and nitrate reactions.
[QCMLS 2021: 6.2.1.5] [Procop 2017, p1237]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 275 · boc2 PDF page 133

question: Which one of the following provides a presumptive identification of a viral infection?
options: cell lysis of sheep red blood cells
explanation:
Many viruses produce changes in infected cells that is called cytopathic effect. Viruses
cannot be visualized but CPE can be detected in specific cell lines. Most laboratories now use
immunologic and molecular methods for ID of viruses, rather than the CPE.
[QCMLS 2021 : 6.6.2] (Mahon 2019, p587-588]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 278 · boc2 PDF page 134

question: The genus of virus associated with anogenital warts, cervical dysplasia and neoplasia is:
explanation:
Human papilloma virus (HPV) infects epithelial tissues throughout the body, including
skin, larynx, and anogenital tissue. Persistent infection with oncogenic types of HPV and
integration of HPV DNA into the cellular genome is a pathway leading to HPV-induced
neoplasia, such as cervical cancer.
[QCMLS 2021: 6.6.7]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 280 · boc2 PDF page 134

question: Encephalitis is most commonly associated with which of the following viruses?
explanation:
Herpes simplex virus is the most common cause of fatal sporadic encephalitis in the
United States.
[QCMLS 2021: 6.6.4.1)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 281 · boc2 PDF page 134

question: Colds and other acute respiratory diseases are most often associated with:
explanation:
Adenovirus infections are common. It causes up to 5% of all respiratory infections, and
the prevalence of infection is higher (up to 14%).
[QCMLS 2021 : 6.6.5]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 282 · boc2 PDF page 134

question: The Epstein-Barr virus is associated with which of the following?
explanation:
The classic clinical syndrome associated with Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection is
infectious mononucleosis. However, in immunocompromised patients, EBV is associated with
posttransplant lymphoproliferative disorders, and malignancies such as Burkitt lymphoma.
[QCMLS 2021: 6.6.4.4)

question: Which of the following agents is the most common cause of pediatric viral gastroenteritis?
explanation:
Rotavirus is the most common cause of viral gastroenteritis in infants and children. It
causes >600,000 deaths annually. Coronavirus causes cold-like infections in adults and a
small percentage of pediatric diarrhea cases. Adenovirus is mostly asymptomatic, causing
a small percentage of pneumonia and gastroenteritis in children. Norwalk virus is the
most common cause of adult viral gastroenteritis and is often responsible for the diarrheal
outbreaks on cruise ships, resorts, or nursing homes.
[QCMLS 2021: 6.7.2.2, 6.6.17) [Mahon 2019, p690, 698, 700]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 284 · boc2 PDF page 134

question:
Hanta or Sin Nombre virus is a Bunyavirus found in the 4 Corners area of the US (Arizona,
New Mexico, Nevada, Colorado). What is the vector?
explanation:
Deer mouse: Peromyscus manicu/atus, or the deer mouse, spreads the virus in its
infected feces. People living in close contact with animals are at a particularly high risk.
Infected individuals develop a pulmonary syndrome.
[QCMLS 2021: 6.6.13] [Mahon 2019, p699-700]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 285 · boc2 PDF page 134

question: Which type of virus causes severe acute respiratory syndrome?
explanation:
Coronavirus: SARS is a severe respiratory disease spread from human to human and
caused by a coronavirus (SARS CoV).
[QCMLS 2021: 6.6.14] [Mahon 2019, p701]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 286 · boc2 PDF page 135

question: What is the animal reservoir of West Nile virus?
explanation:
The host organism is the bird, which passes on the virus through a mosquito vector to
humans.
[QCMLS 2021 : 6.6.16) [Mahon 2019, p703]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 287 · boc2 PDF page 135

question: Which of the following organisms is the causative agent of hand, foot and mouth disease?
explanation:
Coxsackie A & 8 are frequently confused for each other in terms of the diseases that
they cause. Coxsackie A causes hand, foot, and mouth disease, so named for the most
common locations of the lesions. Coxsackie B is responsible for the majority of cases of viral
myocarditis.
[QCMLS 2021: 6.6.12.1) [Mahon 2019, p708]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 288 · boc2 PDF page 135

question:
Which one of the following viruses is responsible for the most common congenital infection in
the United States?
explanation:
CMV: Passed transplacentally, the risk of in utero infection is greatest when the mother
acquires a primary CMV infection while pregnant. The effects from in utero infection can
range from severe to mild.
[QCMLS 2021: 6.6.4.3) [Mahon 2019, p692]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 289 · boc2 PDF page 135

question: Which one of the following clinical syndromes is associated with VZV infection?
explanation:
All the other options are associated with EBV infection; shingles is the only option that is
caused by VZV.
[QCMLS 2021: 6.6.4.2) [Mahon 2019, p815]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 290 · boc2 PDF page 135

question: Which of the following clinical presentations is associated with HHV8?
explanation:
Especially in the immune-compromised patient HHV8 or KSHV is associated with a
number of disease processes, also including primary effusion lymphoma. The etiologic agent
in these cases can be identified by PCR, IHC, or serological means.
[QCMLS 2021 : 6.6.4.7) [Mahon 2019, p695-696]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 291 · boc2 PDF page 135

question:
In a person vaccinated against hepatitis B virus several years prior, which serological marker
would be expected?
explanation:
Anti HBs in serum indicates convalescence or immune status. All of the other choices,
with perhaps the early appearance post vaccination of HBsAg, should not be seen in a
vaccinated person. HBeAg is present during active viral replication. Anti HBc shows early in
the course of disease and shows an acute infection.
[QCMLS 2021: 6.6.9.2) [Mahon 2019, p714-715]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 292 · boc2 PDF page 135

question: The persistence of which marker is the best evidence of chronic HBV infection?
explanation:
The persistence of surface antigen is an excellent indicator of chronicity. With acute
infection and resolution surface antigen peaks 2-3 months post-infection and before
symptoms, but is completely gone before 6 months, to be replaced by anti surface antibody
(HBsAb} and the clinical symptoms of acute hepatitis. In chronic infection the surface antibody
does not appear, while the surface antigen persists.
[QCMLS 2021: 6.6.9.2)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 293 · boc2 PDF page 135

question: Which of the following statements regarding antigenic shift or drift in influenza is correct?
options: antigenic drift is due to point mutations in the H&N genes
antigenic drift is responsible for pandemics of influenza
antigenic shift is responsible for seasonable epidemics of influenza

local annual outbreaks of influenza are often due to antigenic shift
~ ~---'------=~
explanation:
Drift refers to the minor changes that occur due to point mutations. Drift is primarily
responsible for the annual outbreaks and epidemics of influenza. Shift refers to a more major
change due to recombination between different viral subtypes and is most often the cause of
the periodic pandemic infections. It is due to antigenic drift and shift that lifelong immunity to
influenza cannot currently be achieved.
[QCMLS 2021 : 6.6.10.1)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 294 · boc2 PDF page 135

question: This virus is responsible for nearly all cases of infantile respiratory bronchiolitis:
explanation:
RSV is the most common cause of severe lower respiratory tract disease in infants and
young children. Persistence of immunity does not often occur so reinfection is common.
[QCMLS 2021: 6.6.11.4) [Mahon 2019, p707]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 295 · boc2 PDF page 136

question: Which one of the following is a characteristic of hepatitis B virus?
options: hepatitis B infects CD4+ T lymphocytes.
it is an enveloped DNA virus that is primarily a blood-borne pathogen.
this RNA virus is almost always transmitted by the fecal-oral route.
explanation:
It is an enveloped DNA virus that is transmitted through sexual, perinatal, and parenteral
routes. The virus enters the host and travels from the blood to the liver and infects
hepatocytes.
[QCMLS 2021: 6.6.9.2] [Mahon 2019, p713]
C. Parasitology
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 298 · boc2 PDF page 136

question: Primary amoebic encephalitis is caused by:
explanation:
Naeg/eria fowleri is the etiologic agent of primary amoebic encephalitis.
[QCMLS 2021 : 6.4.2.1] [Mahon 2019, p631]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 302 · boc2 PDF page 136

question: The advantage of thick blood smears for malarial parasites is to:
explanation:
The increased amount of blood placed on the slide of a thick smear for blood parasites
increases likelihood to detect parasite.
(QCMLS 2021: 6.4.3.3] [Mahon 2019, p645]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 304 · boc2 PDF page 137

question:
This parasite is transmitted by accidental ingestion of cat feces that contain oocysts and by
ingestion of undercooked meat that has tissue cysts. The parasite is:
explanation:
Cyc/ospora and Cryptosporidium are found in feces and associated with diarrhea.
Trypanosoma cruzi is a hemoflagellate introduced into the human host by the reduviid bug
and causes Chagas disease or heart disease. Toxoplasma is the only choice that is found in
cat feces, and infection often occurs when undercooked meat with tissue cysts is ingested.
[QCMLS 2021: 6.4.3.1] [Mahon 2019, p649-651]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 305 · boc2 PDF page 137

question: Trophozoites of the cyst shown in the image are likely to:
explanation:
The image shows a cyst with more than 4 nuclei, an indication of Entamoeba coli.
Trophozoites of Entamoeba coli demonstrate slow and undefined motility. They do not ingest
RBCs.
[QCMLS 2021: 6.4.2.1) [Mahon 2019, p626, 628)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 309 · boc2 PDF page 138

options: immediately telephone the report of this pathogen to the physician

review the fecal concentration carefully for the presence of other microorganisms that may
be pathogenic

request a new specimen because of the presence of excessive pollen grains

Entamoeba coli is a nonpathogenic protozoan. Its presence indicates the ingestion of
fecally contaminated food or water and should lead to a closer review of the specimen for

[QCMLS 2021 : 6.4.2.1) [Mahon 2019, p626]

explanation:
The image displays the trophozoite form of Giardia duodena/is (syn lamblia), a protozoan
flagellate parasite.
[QCMLS 2021 : 6.4.2.2.1)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 313 · boc2 PDF page 140

question:
A 24-year-old woman, who just returned from vacationing in Lebanon, becomes ill with
diarrhea. The organisms shown in the image are found in her stool. The patient most likely is
suffering from:
explanation:
Diarrhea associated with Giardia duodena/is (syn /amblia) is caused by the consumption
of contaminated water and results in greasy, foul-smelling stools. The image shows both the
trophozoite and cyst forms of Giardia.
[QCMLS 2021 : 6.4.2.2.1) [Mahon 2019, p617J
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 314 · boc2 PDF page 140

question:
Small protozoan cysts are found in a wet mount of sediment from ethyl-acetate concentrated
material. Each cyst has 4 nuclei that do not have peripheral chromatin, and each nucleus has
a large karyosome, which appears as a refractive dot. These oval cysts are most likely:
explanation:
While Entamoeba hartmanni and Endolimax nana are a similar size, E. hartmanni has
similar peripheral chromatin to E. histo/ytica, while E. nana has none. E. histo/ytica cysts are
larger and round when compared to E. nana. Chilomastix is a flagellated protozoan, and has
only 1 nucleus.
[QCMLS 2021: 6.4.2.1) [Mahon 2019, p819]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 316 · boc2 PDF page 140

question: The term "internal autoinfection" is generally used in referring to infections with:
explanation:
Strongy/oides stercoralis rhabditiform larvae are capable of transforming into filariform
(infective) larvae in the intestines of immunocompromised patients. This establishes an
autoinfective cycle.
[QCMLS 2021: 6.4.4.1) [Mahon 2019, p666-667]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 317 · boc2 PDF page 141

question:
A fibrous skin nodule is removed from the back of a patient from Central America.
A microfilaria seen upon microscopic exam of the nodule is most likely:
explanation:
Onchocerca volvulus is the only microfilaria that is detected in the skin snips of patients
with raised skin nodules. The microfilaria of Wuchereria, Brugia and Loa /oa are found in the
blood of infected patients.
(QCMLS 2021: 6.4.4.2)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 318 · boc2 PDF page 141

question: The egg shown in the image is most likely to be found in children suffering from:
explanation:
The most common sign of Enterobius vermicu/aris infection is intense perianal itching.
[QCMLS 2021: 6.4.4.1) [Mahon 2019, p668]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 319 · boc2 PDF page 141

question: The causative agent of cysticercosis is:
explanation:
Humans may become infected with Taenia solium by either ingesting the larval form (in
undercooked pork) or ova. If ova are ingested the parasite cannot complete the life cycle, and
cysticerci encyst in various tissues including the brain.
[QCMLS 2021: 6.4.4.5] [Mahon 2019, p658-659-664]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 322 · boc2 PDF page 142

question:
What is the principal means of distinguishing Entamoeba histolytica from Entamoeba
hartmanni by light microscopy?
options: number of nuclei in cyst form
explanation:
The only morphological difference between the related organisms is the size of the
trophozoite. Entamoeba histolytica is roughly twice the size at 20-30 µm diameter than
Entamoeba hartmanni, which is only 5-10 µm in diameter. Also, though nonspecific,
E. histolytica tends to be the most common trophozoite to contain ingested RBCs.
[QCMLS 2021: 6.4.2.1) [Mahon 2019, p626-628]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 327 · boc2 PDF page 142

question: Which characteristic will identify lodamoeba butschlii?
options: prominent vacuole in the cyst form
presence of up to 8 nuclei in the cyst form
explanation:
/odamoeba biitschlii has a large clear vacuole in the cyst form, with only one nucleus.
Entamoeba hartmanni is small, and Entamoeba coli has up to 8 nuclei in the cyst form.
Multiple amoeba have 4 nuclei in mature cyst.
[QCMLS 2021: 6.4.2.1] [Mahon 2019, p633]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 328 · boc2 PDF page 142

question: The only medically significant ciliate organism is:
explanation:
Pigs are the natural host for Balantidium coli, and humans are "accidental" hosts. The
intestinal infection can be asymptomatic, but it can also cause some diarrhea with nausea
and vomiting. 8. coli is the only ciliate among the choices.
[QCMLS 2021: 6.4.2.3.1] [Mahon 2019, p642-643]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 329 · boc2 PDF page 142

question: Where do Plasmodium sporozoites proliferate?
explanation:
After sporozoites are introduced into the blood stream by an Anopheles mosquito, they
travel to the liver to proliferate. The infected parenchymal cells rupture and release the
merozoites, which infect RBCs.
[QCMLS 2021: 6.4.3.3) [Mahon 2019, p643, 645]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 330 · boc2 PDF page 142

question:
Individuals who lack the Duffy antigen on the surface of their red blood cells are protected
against which species of P/asmodium?
explanation:
The Duffy antigen is the receptor for Plasmodium vivax (as well as P/asmodium know/es!);
therefore, loss of the receptor affords some protection against infection. Sickle cell trait
protects individuals predominantly against P. falciparum, which produces the most deadly
form of malarial disease.
[QCMLS 2021 : 6.4.3.3] [Mahon 2019, p668-669]

Which nematode produces eggs with characteristic hyaline polar plugs at each end,
as in the image?
explanation:
Trichuris, the whipworm, produces barrel-shaped eggs that have"plugs" or thickenings on
each end. It may co-infect with Ascaris.
[QCMLS 2021: 6.4.4.1] [Mahon 2019, p669-670]

question: Which organism is predominantly responsible for visceral larva migrans?
explanation:
Most cases of visceral larva migrans (and ocular larva migrans) are due to
Toxocara canis. A small percentage of cases are due to Toxocara cati. Onchocerca
causes corneal opacities, Ancy/ostoma braziliensis causes cutaneous larva migrans, and
Trypanosoma brucei is the agent for sleeping sickness.
[QCMLS 2021: 6.4.4.3] [Mahon 2019, p656-658]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 334 · boc2 PDF page 143

question: Which organism has the largest egg?
explanation:
Fasciola hepatica (& Fascio/opsis buskt) have the largest human parasite eggs known
( ~150 µm in diameter). The eggs have a nonshouldered operculum and lack an abopercular
knob.
[QCMLS 2021 : 6.4.4.4] [Mahon 2019, p659-660]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 335 · boc2 PDF page 144

question: The eggs of which species of Schistosoma can be isolated from urine?
explanation:
Schistosoma haematobium migrates to the veins of the bladder so eggs are seen in the
urine. S. mansoni goes to the veins of the large intestine, while S. japonicum infects the veins
of the small intestines, but both will shed eggs in the feces. Strongyloides stercoralis is not a
Schistosoma species, but rather a nematode.
[QCMLS 2021: 6.4.4.4] [Mahon 2019, p663]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 336 · boc2 PDF page 144

question: Which one of the following features of Taenia saginata helps distinguish it from T. solium?
options: egg with a radially striated wall
explanation:
The Taenia species have several features to distinguish them from each other. T. saginata
is the beef tapeworm, T. so/ium is the pork tapeworm. T. saginata has an unarmed rostellum,
unlike the armed rostellum of the pork tapeworm. The proglottid of the beef tapeworm has
>13 uterine branches (as visualized by India ink injection), where the pork tapeworm has <13
branches. In addition the pork tapeworm can cause cysticercosis while the beef tapeworm
does not. The eggs of both tapeworms are identical, with thick radially-striated walls.
[QCMLS 2021: 6.4.4.5) [Mahon 2019, p661]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 337 · boc2 PDF page 144

question: Infection by this organism can cause of B12 deficiency:
explanation:
Diphyllobothrium latum is noted for its ability to cause vitamin B12 deficiency by competing
for binding the vitamin. It occurs primarily in people of northern European descent.
[QCMLS 2021: 6.4.4.5) [Mahon 2019, p666]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 338 · boc2 PDF page 144

question: This organism is responsible for hydatid cysts of the liver:
explanation:
The most common definitive host is the dog, where the eggs are found in the feces.
Ingestion of eggs by intermediate hosts, such as sheep or cattle directly causes the disease.
Humans accidentally ingest the eggs (sheepherders). It is seen mostly in sheep-raising
countries or areas of the US. The primary manifestation is hepatic cysts.
[QCMLS 2021 : 6.4.4.5] [Mahon 2019, p636-637]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 339 · boc2 PDF page 144

question: How is Trichomonas vagina/is transmitted?
options: larval stage burrows through the skin
explanation:
Trichomonas vagina/is only has a trophozoite stage, so it is sensitive to the environment.
It is a pathogen of the urogenital tract of men and women. It is one of the most common STDs
worldwide.
[QCMLS 2021 : 6.4.2.2.3] [Mahon 2019, p646)

question:
This parasite has the following characteristics:
banana shaped gametocytes in RBCs
multiple ring forms in RBCs
all RBCs are infected
The identification of the parasite is:
explanation:
Plasmodium vivax and P. ovate are found in enlarged (young) RBCs only, and P. malariae
usually invades older RBCs. P. falciparum invades RBCs of any age, and multiple ring forms
in a single RBC are common. The banana-shaped gametocyte is produced by P falciparum.
(QCMLS 2021 : 6.4.3.3] [Mahon 2019, p652-653]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 341 · boc2 PDF page 144

question: The major features by which molds are routinely categorized are:
options: macroscopic growth characteristics and microscopic morphology
specialized sexual reproductive cells and phialides
explanation:
Macroscopic characteristics and microscopic morphology are observations used for the
routine identification of molds.
(QCMLS 2021: 6.5.1] [Mahon 2019, p609]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 343 · boc2 PDF page 145

question:
Many fungal infections are transmitted to man via inhalation of infectious structures.
Which of the following is usually contracted in this manner?
explanation:
Histop/asma capsulatum is the only choice that is transmitted by inhalation.
[QCMLS 2021: 6.5.2] [Mahon 2019, p608]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 345 · boc2 PDF page 145

question:
Using a fluorescent microscope, a wet preparation of skin tissue reveals fluorescent septate
hyphae. The smear is prepared using:
explanation:
Calcofluor white binds to cellulose and chitin present in fungal cell walls. It flouresces
when exposed to long-wave UV light.
[QCMLS 2021: 6.5.1] [Mahon 2019, p611]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 346 · boc2 PDF page 145

question: The formation of germ tubes presumptively identifies:
explanation:
Candida albicans produces germ tubes.
(QCMLS 2021: 6.5.6.1] [Mahon 2019, p604]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 347 · boc2 PDF page 145

question:
An HIV-positive patient begins to show signs of meningitis. A spinal fluid specimen is collected
and cultured for bacteria and fungus. A budding, encapsulated yeast is recovered. Which
organism is consistent with this information?
explanation:
Cryptococcus neoformans is a cause of meningitis in immunocompromised patients, and
produces a polysaccharide capsule.
[QCMLS 2021 : 6.5.6.2] [Mahon 2019, p604]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 348 · boc2 PDF page 145

question:
The one characteristic by which an unknown Cryptococcus species can be identified as
~t~Y
Cryptococcus neoformans is:
explanation:
Cryptococcus neoformans is the only clinically encountered yeast that is
phenol-oxidase-positive.
[QCMLS 2021: 6.5.6.1] [Mahon 2019, p600, 604]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 350 · boc2 PDF page 146

question:
The morphological characteristics of a yeast grown in rabbit plasma are shown in the image:
The most likely identification of this yeast is:
explanation:
Candida albicans produces tubular structures with no constrictions (germ tubes) when
incubated in rabbit plasma.
[QCMLS 2021 : 6.5.6.1) [Mahon 2019, p613]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 355 · boc2 PDF page 147

question:
Laboratory workers should always work under a biological safety hood when working with
cultures of:
explanation:
The arthroconidia of Coccidioides immitis are highly infectious; cultures must be handled
with care to minimize aerosols.
[QCMLS 2021: 6.5.2.3) [Mahon 2019, p595]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 358 · boc2 PDF page 147

question: Structures important in the microscopic identification of Coccidioides immitis are:
explanation:
The mycelial phase of Coccidioides immitis produces alternating, barrel-shaped
arthrospores.
[QCMLS 2021: 6.5.2.3] [Mahon 2019, p596]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 359 · boc2 PDF page 147

question:
Which of the following is the most useful morphological feature in identifying the mycelial
phase of Histop/asma capsulatum?
explanation:
The presence of tuberculate macroconidia indicates a presumptive identification of
Histoplasma capsulatum. The identification must be confirmed using nucleic acid probes or
exoantigen testing.
[QCMLS 2021: 6.5.2.1] [Mahon 2019, p592]

question: Which of the following is a dimorphic fungus?
explanation:
Dimorphic molds include 8/astomyces, Histoplasma, Coccidioides, Paracoccidioides,
Ta/aromyces (formerly Penicillium) marneffei, Sporothrix.
[QCMLS 2021: 6.5.2.2) [Mahon 2019, p49, 472]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 6 · Question 362 · boc2 PDF page 148

The microscopic structures that are most useful in the identification of dermatophytes are:
1.11.S
explanation:
Dermatophytes include 3 genera that are generally differentiated by their macroconidia
and microconidia formation.
[QCMLS 2021: 6.5.3.3)

[QCMLS 2021: 6.5.3.1, 6.5.3.2) [Mahon 2019, p600]

question:
Which of the following dermatophytes can be identified with its clavate or peg-shaped
microconidia that resemble "birds on a wire"?
explanation:
Trichophyton rubrum have microconidia and of them each has unique morphologic
features. T. rubrum has "birds on a wire" microconidia spaced along hyphae, T. tonsurans has
widely variable microconicia, while T. mentagrophytes has grapelike clusters and occasional
spiral hyphae. Microsporum canis produces large macroconidia that are spindle shaped.
[QCMLS 2021: 6.5.3.3) [Mahon 2019, p604]

question: Which fungal organism is urease+ and phenol oxidase+?
explanation:
All of the organisms mentioned, with the exception of Malassezia, are urease-positive,
but Cryptococcus is the only one that is also phenol-oxidase-positive. The presence of phenol
oxidase can be demonstrated on bird (Niger) seed agar, where the phenol oxidase will
convert the caffeic acid in the agar into melanin pigment, yielding the characteristic brown/
black color.
[QCMLS 2021 : 6.5.6.1) [Mahon 2019, p598]

question: Microbiology-related urgent or critical results include positive:
options: blood cultures, cerebrospinal fluid cultures and acid-fast smears
blood cultures, urine cultures and ova & parasite examinations
cerebrospinal fluid cultures, fungal cultures and ova & parasite examinations
Streptococcus pyogenes throat screens, bronchial washing cultures and fungal cultures
explanation:
Results that may require rapid clinical attention to avoid significant patient morbidity or
mortality are classified as an urgent or critical result. The reporting of urgent/critical results
includes verbally reporting results to a primary care practitioner (eg, the ordering physician)
and documenting that communication. Positive blood cultures, CSF cultures, and acid-fast
smears (possible Mycobacterium tuberculosis) are generally considered critical results. Other
culture results should be reported as soon as useful information becomes available, but do
not require verbal notification of a caregiver. Based on patient population and need, clinical
laboratories determine their own urgent/critical reporting criteria.
(QCMLS 2021: 6.9.2] (Procop 2017, p43]

explanation:

transmission of physician orders, specimen transport and preparation, requisition accuracy,
quality of phlebotomy services, specimen acceptability rates, etc. The variables chosen
should be appropriate to the laboratory's scope of care.
[QCMLS 2021 : 7.6.1.2]

question:
A clean-catch urine is submitted to the laboratory in a plain sterile urine cup for
routine urinalysis and culture. The routine urinalysis is performed first. Three hours later,
the specimen is sent to the microbiology department for culture. The specimen should:
options: be centrifuged, and the supernatant cultured
be rejected due to the time delay
not be cultured if no bacteria are seen
be processed for culture only if the nitrate is positive
explanation:
It is common practice to share samples between the microbiology department and
urinalysis. Ideally, the culture is set up first to prevent contamination. If that is not feasible, the
sample should be aliquotted using aseptic technique, and refrigerated until it can be cultured.
[QCMLS 2021: 7.6.1]

alkaline urine. d is false, ketones are produced by fat metabolism in the patient.

question:
On Monday a patient's hemoglobin determination is 11.3 g/dl (113 g/L), and on Tuesday it
measures 11.8 g/dl (118 g/L). The standard deviation of the method used is ±0.2 g/dl (2 g/L).
Which of these statements can be concluded about the hemoglobin values given?
options: one value probably resulted from laboratory error
there is poor precision; daily quality control charts should be checked
the second value is out of range and should be repeated
there is no significant change in the patient's hemoglobin concentration
explanation:
Standard deviation is a reflection of variance around the mean. In this case, ± 2 SD is
0.4 g/dl below the mean to 0.4 g/dl above the mean or an acceptable range of 0.8 g/dl.
The difference in the patient's hemoglobin determinations on Monday (11.3) and Tuesday
(11.8) is 0.5 g/dl, which is within the acceptable± 2 SD range of 0.8 g/dl.
[QCMLS 2021: 7.3.1.1]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 7 · Question 19 · boc2 PDF page 201

question: Instrument calibration verification is the process of:
options:
assaying quality control materials in the same manner as patient samples to confirm that
the calibration of the instrument is stable throughout the reportable range

determining the closeness of agreement between independent test results obtained under
stipulated conditions

assaying calibration materials in the same manner as patient samples to confirm that the
calibration of the instrument is stable throughout the reportable range

a one-time process completed to confirm instrument performance characteristics before
the interment is used for patient testing
explanation:
Calibration verification involves the use of several specimens with known concentrations
(patient samples, commercial calibrators, proficiency testing material, controls) to ensure the
validity of the calibrator over a wider range of results. Calibration is analogous to "zeroing"
a scale, and calibration verification is analogous to then testing the scale using a series of
known weights. Calibration verification must be carried out at least once every 6 months and
more frequently under some circumstances, eg, after major preventive maintenance.
[QCMLS 2021 : 7.4.2.1)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 7 · Question 20 · boc2 PDF page 201

question:
Specimen stability refers to insignificant increase or decrease in the concentration of an
analyte in a stored specimen. Conditions to be considered when conducting a stability
experiment would not include:
options: effect of temperature and humidity on specimens

specimen transportation conditions (time, temperature, tube orientation, agitation, light
exposure)
maximum storage lime is defined by the date of the earliest-expiring reagent
explanation:
Specimen stability refers to the length of time that a stored specimen will continue to
produce reliable results, and may be assessed for specimens stored at room temperature,
at refrigerator temperature, and/or for frozen specimens. To determine, patient samples are
tested immediately and at intervals under the defined storage conditions. Maximum storage
time is defined as the last time before significant, predefined, variation is noted. For example,
one may choose to use ±2 SD or ±3 SD as defining significant variation.
[QCMLS 2021: 7.4.2.7)

question:
The main goal of a quality control (QC) strategy is to reduce the risk of harm to a patient if an
erroneous result is used for clinical decision making. A QC strategy should be customized to
the test and testing situation. The core focus of a QC strategy centers around:
options: accuracy, precision, and reproducibility of test systems

a measurement procedure's performance capability relative to the quality required, and
validation data
explanation:
A measurement procedure's performance capability relative to the quality required and
validation data, interlaboratory quality control data, and critical control point quality control
are all particular methods used in QC, but measuring accuracy, precision and reproducibility
of tests/test systems are the core foci of QC in the laboratory.

question:
The primary advantage of point-of-care testing (POCT), also known as bedside testing or
near patient testing is:
options: POCT can be performed by nonlaboratorians at a lower cost
the turn-around time for test results is faster
POCT bypasses costly regulatory requirements that apply to testing in a central lab
testing is easier to perform, which reduces the cost of training
explanation:
Laboratory testing performed by nonlaboratory personnel outside of the clinical laboratory,
close to or near the patient is defined at point-of-care testing (POCT). Performing laboratory
testing at the point of care eliminates the time required to transport specimens to the
laboratory, and thus reduces the total turnaround time for testing. POCT is typically performed
by nonlaboratorians and nearly always subject to regulatory and accreditation standards that
vary, depending on the location and test complexity.
{QCMLS 2021: 7.7.12]

laboratories must have a current CUA certificate to submit claims to Medicare or Medicaid

Medicare part A (inpatient coverage) and part B (outpatient coverage) includes prescription
drug coverage
explanation:
A laboratory must have a current CUA certificate to submit claims to Medicare or
Medicaid. Medicare part A helps cover inpatient medical care. Medicare part B helps cover
outpatient services & inpatient physician services according to a fee schedule (fee for

question:
Medical billing codes are used to classify a patient's treatment, diagnosis, and associated
medical supplies. Which of the following is not a primary medical billing code?
explanation:
The Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) was developed in
1996 and became part of the Social Security Act and does not involve medical billing;
The primary purpose of the HIPAA rules is to protect health care coverage for workers
who lose or change jobs. It protects records that can be retrieved by personal identifiers
and prohibits disclosures without written consent unless a specified exception applies.
The International Coding or Classification of Disease (ICD) is a coding system specific to
diagnosis or a medical problem used to establish medical necessity. Current procedural
terminology (CPT) is the coding system that describes procedure(s) performed. The Health
Care Procedural Coding System (HCPCS) describes blood products, medical goods, or
services.
[QCMLS 2021: 7.1.4, 7.1.8)

question:
Which of the following organizations was formed to encourage the voluntary attainment of
uniformly high standards in institutional medical care?
options: The Joint Commission (T JC), formerly known as JCAHO
explanation:
The CDC, HCFA and FDA are organizations created by the US federal government.
The American College of Surgeons (ACS) adopted a one page document titled "The Minimum
Standard for Hospitals" in 1919. In 1950 multiple medical professional organizations joined
ACS as corporate members to create the Joint Commission on Accreditation of Hospitals
to provide voluntary accreditation. Today "The Joint Commission" sets standards by which
healthcare is measured and accredits institutions and laboratories worldwide.

question:
Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments of 1988 (CLIA) was established to provide
oversight to:
options: research labs performing testing on human specimens
waived point-of-care testing by nonlaboratory personnel
all US facilities or sites performing patient testing to diagnose, prevent, or treat disease
explanation:
CUA regulations include federal standards applicable to all U.S. facilities or sites that
test human specimens for health assessment or to diagnose, prevent, or treat disease.
Exceptions to the CUA regulations exist for certain testing, including employment-related drug
testing by SAMSHA certified laboratories, testing performed for forensic purposes (criminal
investigations), and research or surveillance testing performed on human specimens in which
patient-specific results are not reported (if the results are not used for diagnosis or treatment
decisions).
[QCMLS 2021: 7 .1.1] [https://www.cdc.gov/clia/about.htmlj

question: According to CLIA, who is responsible for classifying lab test complexity?

explanation:

complex: waived tests, moderate complexity tests, and high complexity tests. Diagnostic tests
are categorized as waived based on the premise that they are simple to use, and there is little
chance the test will provide wrong information or cause harm if it is done incorrectly.
[QCMLS 2021: 7.1.1.1] [42 CFR 493.17]

question:
If your lab performs a test for which there is no commercially available control of proficiency
test material, which of the following is acceptable as an alternative method for determining
analytic testing reliability?
options: you do not have to do anything if there is nothing available
make an internal lab control from a previous negative and positive
have 2 technologists perform the test independently
explanation:
For tests for which CAP does not require enrollment in PT, the laboratory must at
least semi-annually 1) participate in external PT, or 2) exercise an alternative performance
assessment system for determining the reliability of analytical testing. Appropriate alternative
performance assessment procedures include participation in an external PT program;
participation in an ungraded/educational PT program; split sample analysis with another
laboratory, split sample analysis with an established in-house method, use of assayed
materials, clinical validation by chart review, or other suitable and documented means as
determined by the medical laboratory director.
[QCMLS 2021: 7.5.3.2) [CAP 2020, COM.10500]

question: A paper or electronic report of lab results must include:
options: the name of the person who collected the specimen
the name and address of the testing laboratory
explanation:
CAP General Checklist: The paper or electronic report includes the following elements:
• Name and address of testing laboratory (see note below)
• Patient name and identification number, or unique patient identifier
• Name of physician of record, or legally authorized person ordering test, as appropriate
• Date and time of specimen collection, when appropriate
• Date of release of report (if not on the report, this information should be readily accessible)
• Time of release of report, if applicable (if not on the report, this information should be readily
accessible)
• Specimen source, when applicable
• Test result(s) (and units of measurement, when applicable)
• Reference intervals, as applicable (see note below)
• Conditions of specimen that may limit adequacy of testing.
[QCMLS 2021: 7.6.2.2] [CAP 2020, GEN.41096]

question:
A quality management system (QMS) is a system for designing, implementing, maintaining,

competence assessment of testing personnel. Training is not required:
options: for newly hired, transferred or promoted personnel
when new testing platforms are implemented
when there is a change in the medical director of the lab
when an employee demonstrates repeated performance issues
explanation:

review of results by a qualified technologist or technician
explanation:

question:
Proficiency testing (PT) and alternate assessment procedures (AAP) are valuable tools in the
quality improvement process. PT/AAP processes are a sequence of activities that enables
the laboratory to monitor and assess PT performance to meet mandatory regulatory and
accreditation requirements for external assessment of examination methods. Which PT/AAP
activity is allowable?
options: sharing PT results within a multi-laboratory system before result submission
interlaboratory communication after PT testing is complete
interlaboratory communication after PT results are submitted

sending PT samples to another laboratory for reflexing testing using the same process as
used for patient testing
explanation:
The sample must not be sent out of the laboratory, even if under normal circumstances,
confirmatory testing might be sought outside the laboratory. There must be no communication
with other laboratories that do not share the same CUA certificate prior to submitting
PT results. After the results have been submitted, however, even successful PT performance
can be a source of useful information. If bias, drift, or shift implied by the reported SDs,
Cembrowski & colleagues recommend a Westgard-like method of evaluating the data.
[QCMLS 2021: 7.5.3.1)

question:
When PT materials are not available, the laboratory needs to develop alternate assessment
procedure (AAP) that includes all except which element?
options: determine the frequency for performing the AAP
grade the target value and the maximum tolerable deviation from that target value
define the criteria for acceptable performance
explanation:
Proficiency testing providers have a large data set of enrollee's results to develop the
target value and the maximum tolerable deviation from that target value. Laboratories using
AAP procedures do not have that luxury, and must determine their own unique criteria for
acceptable performance.
[QCMLS 2021: 7 .5.3.2]

question:
The FDA is responsible for regulating companies who manufacture, repackage, relabel, or
import medical devices sold in the United States. Which of the following statements related
medical devices and biologics used in a clinical laboratory is true?
options:
laboratories must report instrument malfunctions directly to the manufacturer, not to the
federal government
laboratory-developed assays are exempt from FDA medical device requirements

laboratory tests performed with analyte-specific reagents require a specific statement to be
included in the patient report with the test result
Medicare does not reimburse testing performed with analyte-specific reagents
explanation:
The FDA considers analyte-specific reagents (ASRs) to be medical devices and therefore
subject to its regulation; under this authority, it published "the ASR rule" in 1997. Reports
of test results must include the statement, 'This test was developed, and its performance
characteristics determined by (laboratory name). It has not been cleared or approved by the
US Food and Drug Administration."
[QCMLS 2021: 7.1.2.1)

question:
The False Claims Act prohibits the billing of fraudulent claims for medical services including
laboratory testing. Which of the following statements is true?
options: laboratories are allowed for to bill for testing if ordered by an authorized individual
unintentional billing errors does not put a healthcare institution at risk of losing funding
unintentional billing errors caused by a mistake is considered fraud
billing for a service not performed is considered billing waste
explanation:
The False Claims Act prohibits the submission of false or fraudulent claims for medical
services to a federal government health care program. Many billing errors are simply
unintentional mistakes. Ignoring mistakes, choosing not to fix them, and failing to prevent
them from recurring could be considered a false claim by government payers such as
Medicare and Medicaid, and the health care organization risks the loss of funding from
these programs and significant financial penalties. Waste refers to practices that result in
unnecessarily increased costs because of mismanagement or overuse of medical services.
[QCMLS 2021: 7.1.5)

Which of the following agencies uniformly regulates the packaging and shipping of specimens

DOT, IATA and USPS have different rules regarding shipping of biological specimens and

ntle VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 made it illegal to discriminate against someone on the
bases of race, color, religion, national origin, and sex. The Civil Rights Act:
explanation:
Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (Title VII) states that it is illegal to discriminate

question:
Laboratories are required to perform and document analytical validation of each test method
or instrumental system before use in patient testing. Which of the following are required
elements of a test validation experiment?
options: units of measure, reportable range and linearity
specimen collection container(s), precision, and frequency that the test will be performed
accuracy, reference intervals and analytic specificity including interfering substances
analytic sensitivity, linearity and instrument selection
explanation:
Method validation consists of experiments to prove both the clinical value of a test
and performance characteristics. Verification involves the following elements: precision,
accuracy, reportable range, reference intervals, analytical sensitivity, and analytical specificity.
Validation has all the components of verification and also has greater statistical power
(usually involves larger sample numbers), and assessment of additional parameters (clinical
sensitivity, clinical specificity, and positive predictive value).
[QCMLS 2021: 7.4.1, 17.2]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 7 · Question 58 · boc2 PDF page 206

question: Test precision is verified by:
options: comparing results from analyzing the same specimens on multiple analyzers over time

repeat measurements of samples of multiple concentrations within run and between runs
performed over a period of time
comparing results to a definitive or reference method for the same analyte

comparing results of multiple specimens analyzed by multiple individuals and multiple
instruments
explanation:
Precision refers to the reproducibility of a result. Precision is verified by replicating
measurements on the same specimens, both simultaneously (within run precision) and
consecutively (between run precision).
[QCMLS 2021: 7.4.2.2]

question:
A reference interval is the interval between and including the lower and upper reference limits.
Determining the reference intervals that will be reported with a test result is a required
element of test method validation. Which of the following is not true when establishing
reference values for a new analyte is being considered?
options: list of analytical interferences and sources of biological variability from literature
establishment of selection or exclusion criteria (eg, age, sex, health)

determine the appropriate number of reference individuals in consideration of desired
confidence limits
lower and upper limits must be established for each analyte
explanation:
Reference ranges or reference intervals are established based on where 95% of healthy
individuals would fall. Reference intervals must be stratified based on population-dependent
variables such as age, sex, and in some cases, ethnicity. A reference population is a group of
healthy individuals demographically comparable to the patient population. CLSI recommends
testing at least 120 such individuals, applying exclusion criteria as appropriate, and controlling
preanalytical variables. The reference interval may be taken as the central 95% of values
or as all values falling within +2 SD and -2 SD. Some analytes (eg, serum prostate specific
antigen) have no relevant lower limit.
[QCMLS 2021 : 7.3.1.8, 7.3.1.9)

A technician is asked to clean out the chemical reagent storeroom and discard any reagents

options: discard chemicals into biohazard containers where they will later be autoclaved
pour reagents down the drain, followed by flushing of water
consult SOS sheets for proper disposal
explanation:
SOS is an OSHA required document that provides information such as physical data

question: A gallon of xylene waste should be:
options: allowed to evaporate in an open room
disposed of with nonincinerated regulated medical waste
disposed of as an EPA hazardous waste through a licensed waste hauler
explanation:
Xylene must be disposed of as an EPA hazardous waste through a licensed waste hauler.
Flushing down the sink and deliberate evaporation are prohibited as unsafe disposal and
work practices. Xylene is not a regulated medical waste. However, if regulated medical waste
and chemicals are mixed together in processing, the resulting waste should be disposed of as

question:
A technologist, who has been routinely working with hazardous chemicals, begins to notice
symptoms of persistent headaches after exposure to these chemicals. What is the first action
the technologist should take?
options: seek independent medical consultation and evaluation
continue to perform work assignment to see if symptoms persist
acquire involved SOS to investigate signs and symptoms
explanation:
The first course of action should be to report the situation to a supervisor, which
always is the first step in any potential workplace exposure of any kind. It is the employer's
responsibility to provide a medical consultation and evaluation free of charge to employees,
who are involved in potential workplace exposures. Early recognition, evaluation and
treatment is key to preventing further exposure and exacerbation of symptoms. Acquiring the
SOS would be part of the supervisor-directed investigation and secondary to reporting the
situation to supervisor.
[QCMLS 2021: 7.8.3) [OSHA 2004]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 7 · Question 73 · boc2 PDF page 208

question:
When an employee reports signs and symptoms of a chemical exposure, the employer should
suggest a medical consultation and evaluation, which is paid by the:
options: employee using the employee's personal benefit time
employer using the employee's personal benefit time
employer on work time without loss of pay
employee on work time without loss of pay
explanation:
The medical consultation and evaluation of a chemical exposure should be paid by the

question:
When initial or baseline chemical exposure monitoring required by OSHA for substances like
formaldehyde or xylene is performed and the results are within permissible exposure limits,
repeat monitoring should be performed:
options: when procedures or equipment surrounding use of the specific chemical change
explanation:
If results of initial or baseline chemical exposure monitoring required by OSHA are within
permissible exposure limits, repeat monitoring should be performed when procedures or
equipment surrounding use of the specific chemical change. If the baseline monitoring was
not within permissible exposure or action limits initially, periodic subsequent monitoring
would be required. However, since the permissible limits in this case were not exceeded,
subsequent monitoring only needs to be performed again if changes are made. Therefore,
the other distractors are incorrect.
(QCMLS 2021: 7.8.3)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 7 · Question 75 · boc2 PDF page 208

question: An example of personal protective equipment (PPE) for handling hazardous chemicals is:

question: When working with sharp equipment and objects, use a:
options: double-glove technique with specimen handling gloves
paper towel or gauze as a barrier
explanation:
It is recommended to use a mechanical device when working with sharp equipment
and objects. Double-glove technique and use of gauze or paper towel as a barrier provide
inadequate protection against needlestick injuries. The two-handed technique leads to more
recapping injuries than does using a one-handed technique.

question:
For safe use and handling of liquid nitrogen:
MlS
options: shield all skin and use a face shield
store cylinders in a horizontal position in a cool dry place
explanation:
When working with liquid nitrogen, one should shield all skin and use a face shield.
Cryogenic gloves, such as Zetex gloves, should be used, because chemically-resistant gloves
are not protective against liquid nitrogen. Cylinders should be stored near good ventilation in
an upright position, not horizontally.

question: Incident reports for occupational injury or illness should:
options: include information on the employee's past medical history
be filed only for incidents involving serious injury or illness
be filed for all incidents including near miss incidents
not be retained after review by a safety committee or officer
explanation:
Incident reports should be filed for all incidents, including near miss incidents. All incidents
require an incident report be filed, not only those resulting in serious injury. The employee's
medical history is confidential, and should not be required. Incident reports need to be
maintained for a defined period of time even after they have been reviewed.
[QCMLS 2021: 7 .1.9)

question: All laboratory instruments should:

have safety checks performed initially and then every 6 months

be connected to multiple outlet adapters
- - - - - -
explanation:
All laboratory instruments should be grounded or double insulated. Repairs should not
be conducted while connected to facility wiring. Safety checks should be performed initially,
annually and whenever repairs are made. Multiple outlet adapters are unsafe and should not
be used in the laboratory.

question:
If areas of the laboratory are designated as "clean" or "contaminated," it is appropriate for a
technologist to:
options: clean technical area bench tops after spills and on a weekly basis
wear a lab coat in the break or lunch room
apply lip balm in a contaminated area
touch a "contaminated" area phone with ungloved hands if hands are washed afterward
explanation:
A technologist may touch a "contaminated" area phone with ungloved hands provided
hands are washed afterward. Bench tops are to be cleaned at the end of each shift as well as
after spills; weekly cleaning is inadequate. Personal protective equipment, such as a lab coat,
should be removed prior to leaving a "contaminated" area. Cosmetics and lip balm must not
be applied in a "contaminated" area.
[QCMLS 2021: 7.8.11.1, 7.8.9.1]

question: What type of identification system does this symbol represent?

material identification, such as HMIS® or NFPA 704. All other choices are incorrect. Physical

label at all, and there is more appropriate signage for radiation. If a chemical is radioactive,

question: Flammable and combustible liquids in containers 2:5 gallons should be stored in:
options: a flammable safety cabinet vented to room air
explanation:
Containers of 5 gallons or more or flammable or combustible liquids should be stored
in an approved safety can. Flammable safety cabinets should not be vented to room air.
Flammable and combustible liquids that require refrigeration are only to be stored in an
explosion-proof refrigerator. Hazardous substances, particularly of that volume, should not be
stored in a fume hood.
[QCMLS 2021: 7.8.4.5]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 7 · Question 86 · boc2 PDF page 210

question: After receiving appropriate training, the first step in using a fire extinguisher is to:
options: sweep the flow of the hose from side to side
squeeze the top handle or lever
aim the hose at the base of the fire
explanation:
The first step is to pull the pin. The mnemonic "PASS" indicates the correct sequence of
actions: 1) pull the pin, 2) aim the hose, 3) squeeze the lever, and 4) sweep the flow.
[QCMLS 2021: 7.8.5]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 7 · Question 87 · boc2 PDF page 210

question: To help prevent electrical fires in healthcare facilities:
options: use multiple outlet or gang plug adapters
tape over worn wiring with certified electrical tape
use only Underwriters Laboratories (UL) or other safety-agency-rated electrical equipment
explanation:
Only UL or other safety agency-rated electrical equipment should be used in healthcare
facilities. Multiple outlet or gang plug adapters are not to be used. No requirement exists to
change circuit breakers annually. Worn wiring must be replaced rather than repaired with tape.
[QCMLS 2021 : 7.8.7]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 7 · Question 88 · boc2 PDF page 210

question:
In addition to keeping the load close to your body and tightening your abdominal muscles
when lifting heavy boxes of supplies, it is important to bend at the:
options: waist; lift with legs and buttocks
knees and hips; lift with legs and buttocks
knees and hips; lift with arms and back
waist; twist your body when lifting
explanation:
When lifting heavy objects, one should bend at the knees and hips, lift with legs and
buttocks. One should not bend at the waist, lift with the back, or twist because these motions
are more likely to result in injury.
[QCMLS 2021: 7.8.14)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 7 · Question 89 · boc2 PDF page 210

question: The best way to prevent or relieve symptoms of carpal tunnel syndrome is to:
options:
raise arms and bend wrists downward
f,ILS
bend back and neck slightly forward
maintain wrists in a neutral position
explanation:
Maintain wrists in a neutral position to prevent or relieve carpal tunnel syndrome
symptoms. Ergonomically incorrect positions include arms raised and wrists bent downward,
and back bent and neck forward. The first course of action would be to evaluate posture, body
mechanics and adjustment of chair and keyboard prior to facility redesign.
[QCMLS 2021: 7.8.14)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 7 · Question 90 · boc2 PDF page 210

question: Class C fires involve:
options:
electrical equipment
:~v during his/her work assignment. What is the best first action to be taken?
explanation:
Class C fires involve electrical equipment. Fires involving paper, wood, and plastics are
class A, while fires involving flammable liquids (including grease, oil, xylene, and alcohol)
would be class B fires.
[QCMLS 2021: 7.8.5)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 7 · Question 91 · boc2 PDF page 211

question: A laboratory employee identifies arm and neck pain after performing repetitive movements
options: report to and discuss issue with supervisor
continue to perform work assignment and see if it improves
make an appointment with his/her personal physician
explanation:
Arm and neck pain after repetitive motion in the workplace should be reported to and
discussed with the supervisor. Pain should never be ignored, and early intervention with
ergonomic injuries is important. The scenario appears to be a work-related issue, and the
employee is entitled to an employer-provided medical evaluation, if indicated. Changing or
adjusting the workstation is a secondary action, which should be done in consultation with the
supervisor and a trained ergonomics specialist.
[QCMLS 2021 : 7.8.14) [CLSI 2007]
