source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 7 · Question 92 · boc2 PDF page 211

question: An example of personal protective equipment (PPE) is:
explanation:
A lab coat is an example of personal protective equipment (PPE). Safety cabinets,
eyewash stations, and safety showers are examples of engineering controls, not PPE.
[QCMLS 2021: 7.8.4.1)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 7 · Question 93 · boc2 PDF page 211

question:
Gloves worn in the laboratory for specimen processing must be removed and hands washed
when:
options: answering the telephone in the technical work area
carrying a specimen outside the technical work area through "clean" areas
answering the telephone in a designated "clean" area
after handling specimens from known isolation precaution patients
explanation:
Gloves must be removed before answering the telephone in a designated "clean" area,
and hands washed afterward. Gloves do not need to be removed in the technical work
area. It is essential to keep gloves on during specimen transportation, even through "clean"
areas, such as the hallways. Care should be taken not to touch anything in the clean areas.
Gloves do not need to be changed after handling isolation precaution patient specimens
unless known contamination has occurred, which is the same for any patient specimen under
"standard precautions."
[QCMLS 2021 : 7.8.9.1)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 7 · Question 94 · boc2 PDF page 211

question: Safety glasses, face shields or other eye and face protectors must be worn when:
options: working with caustic or toxic materials
processing specimens using a splash barrier
explanation:
Safety glasses or face shields must be worn when working with caustic or toxic materials.
It is not required practice to use eye and face protection when viewing culture plates,
processing specimens using a splash barrier, or being present in technical work area unless
working with caustic or toxic materials.
(QCMLS 2021: 7 .8.11]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 7 · Question 95 · boc2 PDF page 211

question: To prevent injury, a safe lab work practice is to:
options: store well-wrapped food in the supply refrigerator
wear contact lenses for eye protection
explanation:
Long hair and jewelry should be secured to avoid contamination with biohazards or
physical injury. The other choices are not safe or acceptable work practices: food should not
be stored in supply refrigerators at all, contact lenses should not be worn in laboratories, and
open weaved shoes are a spill hazard.
[QCMLS 2021: 7.8.11.1)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 7 · Question 96 · boc2 PDF page 211

question: Safe handling and disposal of laboratory generated infectious waste require:
options: thorough mixing of infectious and noninfectious waste
separation of infectious and noninfectious waste
explanation:
Knowledgeable personnel separate waste into designated categories (eg, chemical,
routine, infectious) at the point of generation to reduce disposal costs and minimize employee
exposure to hazardous materials.
[QCMLS 2021 : 7.8.10)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 7 · Question 97 · boc2 PDF page 211

question:
Which of the following is the best choice for decontaminating bench tops contaminated by the
AIDS virus?
explanation:
A 10% solution of bleach is an effective and economical disinfectant, which inactivates
HBV in 10 minutes and HIV in 2 minutes.
[QCMLS 2021: 7.8.9) [Henry 2017, p9-10)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 7 · Question 98 · boc2 PDF page 211

question: The safest method of disposing of hypodermic needles is:
options: recap the needle with its protective sheath prior to discarding
cut the needle with a special device before disposal

discard the needle in an impermeable container without other handling immediately after
use

drop the needle in the waste basket immediately after use
- - - - - -
explanation:
The simplest method of disposing of needles is to dispose of the entire collection device
into a container reserved for sharps.
(QCMLS 2021: 7.8.9.2)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 7 · Question 99 · boc2 PDF page 211

question: Precautions for health care workers dealing with patients or patient specimens include:
options: mouth pipetting when specimens lack a "Precaution" label
reinserting needles into their original sheaths after drawing blood from a patient
wearing a mask and disposable gown to draw blood
prompt cleaning of blood spills with a disinfectant solution such as sodium hypochlorite
explanation:
Blood spills must be cleaned up and decontaminated by personnel using the proper PPE.
[QCMLS 2021: 7.8.9.1)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 7 · Question 100 · boc2 PDF page 212

question:
Infection rate is highest for laboratory professionals exposed to blood and body fluids
containing:
explanation:
Hepatitis B infection is a global public health problem and is one of the most common
infectious diseases in the world.
[QCMLS 2021 : 7.8.9.1)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 7 · Question 101 · boc2 PDF page 212

question:
Which of the following forms of exposure places a technologist at the highest risk for infection
with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)?
options: ingestion (eg, mouth pipetting of positive serum)
splash (eg, infected serum spill onto intact skin)
explanation:
The 3 modes of HIV transmission are through intimate sexual contact, contact with blood,
and perinatal. Needlestick injury falls under the second mode, and poses, on average, a 0.3%
risk of transmission.
[QCMLS 2021: 7.8.9.2)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 7 · Question 102 · boc2 PDF page 212

question: Which disinfectant inactivates HIV and HBV?
explanation:
A 10% solution of bleach is an effective and economical disinfectant, which inactivates
HBV in 10 minutes and HIV in 2 minutes.
[QCMLS 2021 : 7.8.9.1) [Henry 2017, p9-10]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 7 · Question 103 · boc2 PDF page 212

question:
Filters generally used in biological safety cabinets to protect the laboratory worker from
particulates and aerosols generated by microbiology manipulations are:
explanation:
Microbiological hazards are contained using a biological safety cabinet with the air
exhausting through a HEPA filter.
[QCMLS 2021 : 7.8.9.3) [Henry 2017, p8-10)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 7 · Question 104 · boc2 PDF page 212

question: What is the single most effective method to prevent nosocomial spread of infection?
options: perform frequent and appropriate hand hygiene
explanation:
Performing frequent and appropriate hand hygiene is the most effective method to prevent
nosocomial infection. The other choices are methods for preventing spread of infection, but
are not the most effective method.
[QCMLS 2021: 7.8.11.1]
laboratory Operations
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 7 · Question 105 · boc2 PDF page 212

question: Contaminated needles and syringes without safety self-sheathing devices should be:
options: sheared by a needle cutter or bent
discarded directly into an appropriate sharps container
explanation:
Needles without self-sheathing devices discard directly into an appropriate sharps
container, to avoid undo contact with the sharp. Cutting or bending needles are a prohibited
practices. Needle recapping or removal is not preferred, but if required, it must be done using
mechanical devices or for recapping only using a one-handed technique.
[QCMLS 2021: 7.8.9.2]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 7 · Question 106 · boc2 PDF page 212

question: Use of "standard" (universal) precautions minimizes exposure to:
explanation:
"Standard" precautions are designed to minimize exposure to bloodborne pathogens.
[QCMLS 2021: 7.8.9.3]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 7 · Question 107 · boc2 PDF page 212

question: After an accidental needle stick with a contaminated needle, the first action should be to:
options: apply antiseptic ointment to the wound

thoroughly wash the wound with soap and water
-------=-----=----
- -
explanation:
The primary action after an accidental needlestick is to thoroughly wash the wound with
soap and water. The other choices are secondary, not primary actions.
[QCMLS 2021: 7.8.9.2]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 7 · Question 108 · boc2 PDF page 212

question:
What is the most likely mode of transmission for bloodborne pathogens in laboratory acquired
infections?
explanation:
Parenteral inoculation of blood is the most likely mode of bloodborne pathogen
transmission. The other choice are unlikely transmission modes for bloodborne pathogens.
[QCMLS 2021: 7.8.9.2]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 7 · Question 109 · boc2 PDF page 213

question:
Which infectious agent is considered to be the primary occupational health hazard regarding
transmission of bloodborne pathogens?
explanation:
Hepatitis Bis the bloodborne pathogen most likely to be transmitted in an occupational
setting.
[QCMLS 2021: 7.8.9.3]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 7 · Question 110 · boc2 PDF page 213

question:
When processing specimens for mycobacterial testing, what specific engineering control must
be used?
explanation:
Mycobacteria must be processed using a biological safety cabinet. Horizontal laminar
flow hoods are used for pharmacy and other "clean room" functions. Barrier protection does
not provide adequate respiratory protection, and fume hoods are used for chemical, not
biohazard, control.
[QCMLS 2021: 7.8.9.3]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 7 · Question 111 · boc2 PDF page 213

question: Hepatitis B vaccine is:
options: must be provided by the employer free of charge
recommended only when an exposure incident occurs
explanation:
Hepatitis B vaccine must be provided by the employer free of charge, but it is a series
of 3, not a single injection. The hepatitis vaccine is recommended for high-risk employees
upon initial employment, not just when an exposure occurs, yet it is not a mandatory
vaccination.
[QCMLS 2021: 7.8.9.2]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 7 · Question 112 · boc2 PDF page 213

question:
When cleaning up a small (5 ml) blood spill on the countertop, the first step after donning
appropriate personal protective equipment is to:
options: flood the area with an appropriate intermediate to high-level disinfectant
absorb the spill with disposable absorbent material
clean the area with an aqueous detergent solution
explanation:
The first step in cleaning a small spill is to absorb the spill with disposable absorbent
material. Immediately flooding the area with disinfectant should be avoided, as it may create
aerosolization. It is unnecessary to evacuate the area for 30 minutes due to the size and
nature of the spill. The area should be first cleaned with a disinfectant, not a detergent.
[QCMLS 2021: 7 .8.9.1]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 7 · Question 113 · boc2 PDF page 213

question: The most effective disinfectant recommended for bloodborne pathogens is:
explanation:
Sodium hypochlorite is a disinfectant, but alcohol, chorhexidine and povidone-iodine are
antiseptics, not disinfectants.
[QCMLS 2021: 7.8.9.1]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 7 · Question 114 · boc2 PDF page 213

question:
Which of the following microbial agents do not respond to the general rules regarding
microbial inactivation and decontamination?
explanation:
Transmissible spongiform encephalopathy agents (prions), such as Creutzfeldt-Jakob
disease, do not respond to the general rules of inactivation and decontamination. These
agents are not disinfected or inactivated through conventional means for other microbial
agents, as do M. tuberculosis, smallpox, Bacillus anthracis, or Coccidiodes immitis.
[QCMLS 2021: 7.8.9.1]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 7 · Question 115 · boc2 PDF page 213

question:
When processing patient blood specimens and handling other potentially infectious material,
the best choice of gloves is:
explanation:
Single-use disposable gloves are the best choice for processing blood specimens or other
potentially infectious material. Reusable utility gloves are not ideal or the best choice, but
could be used if properly decontaminated after use and inspected for punctures or tears prior
to reuse. Latex gloves should be avoided because of potential sensitization to the latex and
the development of a latex allergy.
[QCMLS 2021 : 7.8.11.1]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 7 · Question 116 · boc2 PDF page 213

question:
While processing patient specimens, a technologist splashes a few small drops of a bronchial
wash specimen on his/her gloves. The first action should be to:
options: wash the gloves with antiseptic/soap and water
continue to wear the gloves until grossly contaminated or leaving the area
wash the gloves with an appropriate disinfectant
change gloves and wash hands with antiseptic/soap and water
explanation:
When gloves become contaminated by even a small amount of potentially infective
material, one should change gloves and wash hands with antiseptic soap and water.
Continuing to wear contaminated gloves, or washing the gloves, are inappropriate practices.
[QCMLS 2021: 7.8.11.1]

question: Regulated medical waste refers to:
explanation:
Infectious waste is referred to as "regulated medical waste."
[QCMLS 2021: 7.8.9.1]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 7 · Question 119 · boc2 PDF page 214

question: A laboratory safety program includes engineering controls such as:
options: biosafety hoods, chemical fume hoods and approved safety policies
sound dampening materials and radiation shielding
explanation:
PPE (gloves and gowns), hand hygiene and safety policies are examples of administrative
controls that protect the user but not the environment.
[QCMLS 2021 : 7.8.4.2] [CLSI 2004, GP26:A3]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 7 · Question 120 · boc2 PDF page 214

question: The first step to be taken when attempting to repair a piece of electronic equipment is:
options: reset all the printed circuit boards
explanation:
Safety guidelines indicate that before attempting to solve any trouble shooting steps for
any equipment, it is necessary to turn the power off for the instrument. This step is necessary
to prevent any possible electric shock.
[QCMLS 2021 : 7.8.7]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 7 · Question 121 · boc2 PDF page 214

question:
Which of the following should be considered when packaging and transporting biological
specimens and microorganisms?
options: specimen and/or organism type and !ability and hazardous materials

laws and regulations depending on mode of transport and whether the shipment is local,
interstate, or international
current OSHA certification for shipping biological specimens
explanation:
The US Department of Transportation (DOT), United States Post Office (USPS) and the
International Air Transport Association have various requirements for packaging and shipping
of biological specimens, infectious agents, and hazardous materials. OSHA regulates
workplace exposures, but does not certify shippers of hazardous materials.
[QCMLS 2021: 7.1.6) [Tietz 2015, p82, 86]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 7 · Question 122 · boc2 PDF page 214

question:
Needles, scalpels, broken glass, and other sharp objects should be handled with extreme
caution. Safe sharps practice does not include the following element:
options: placing used microtome blade into a labeled, puncture-resistant container
disposing of glass bottles in a closed cardboard box to capture shards if broken
use needles with a safety mechanism built into the needle

autoclaving discarded needles to destroy potentially infective agents
-------=----=-----~
explanation:
Broken, cracked, chipped, and/or flawed glassware should be removed from service to
prevent injury and disposed of in a puncture-proof container. Sharps pose both physical and
biological hazards. Safety-engineered mechanical devices and safe work practices should
be used to prevent accidental injury and/or exposure. Reusable instruments should be
decontaminated by using a combination of chemical and autoclaving methods before cleaning
in a washer and routine sterilization. Disposable needles and blades should be discarded in
designated sharps containers, and are not autoclaved.
[QCMLS 2021 : 7.8.8, 7.8.9.1]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 7 · Question 123 · boc2 PDF page 214

question:
Laboratories are required to ensure compliance with applicable national, federal, state, and
local laws and regulations. One of these requirements relates to public health surveillance
notifiable conditions. The requirements vary depending on location. Examples of notifiable
conditions include:
options: infectious diseases, including sexually transmitted disease
environmental exposure, eg, blood lead levels at defined levels
explanation:
Public health surveillance programs require reporting of certain conditions to identify
and control sources of infection or disease, prevent disease, and describe health
trends. Examples include various infectious diseases and lead contamination. Reporting
requirements vary by state. Notifications must be documented and disclosures of personal
health information (PHI) must be tracked. Mouth pipetting is a prohibited laboratory work
practice but not a notifiable condition.
[QCMLS 2021: 7.6.2.4]
B. Emergency Procedures
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 7 · Question 124 · boc2 PDF page 215

question:
A technologist spilled 10 gallons of formaldehyde on the floor. After determining the chemical
poses a significant health hazard, the first action step would be to:
options: control the spill with appropriate absorbent material
explanation:
The primary response should be to evacuate the area. The other choices are secondary
responses after evacuating the area.
[QCMLS 2021: 7.8.12]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 7 · Question 125 · boc2 PDF page 215

question:
According to OSHA, what type of warning sign should be posted in an area where an
immediate hazard exists and where special precautions are necessary?
explanation:
A "Danger" sign is required where immediate hazards are present. The other choices are
incorrect and used for the other purposes as listed in the choices. The word immediate is the
key to choosing the correct answer.
[QCMLS 2021: 7.8.1.1]

question: For fire safety and prevention:
options: fire drills should be announced and practiced in advance
hallways and corridors should be clear and free of obstruction at all times
only one exit is necessary in laboratories that contain an explosion hazard
hazard evaluations only need to be done prior to initiation of clinical operations
explanation:
Hallways and corridors must be clear and free of obstruction at all times for fire safety and
prevention. Fire drills should not be announced or practiced in advanced. Laboratories larger
than 1000 square feet and/or contain explosion hazards require 2 exits.
[QCMLS 2021: 7.8.5]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 7 · Question 127 · boc2 PDF page 215

question: A fire occurs in the laboratory. The first course of action is to:
options: contain the fire by closing doors
explanation:
Persons must be removed from immediate danger as the first course of action; the
other choices are secondary actions. The sequence of actions after removing persons from
immediate danger is to pull the fire alarm, contain the fire, and evacuate the area, if required.
[QCMLS 2021 : 7.8.5]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 7 · Question 128 · boc2 PDF page 215

question:
An electrical equipment fire breaks out in the laboratory. Personnel have been removed from
immediate danger, the alarm has been activated. What is the next action to be taken?
options: contain the fire by closing doors
extinguish fire with type A extinguisher
lock all windows and doors in the immediate area
explanation:
The next correct step is to contain the fire by closing the doors. Evacuation of the facility
is the last action to be taken and only if indicated. A type A extinguisher is for paper, wood
and plastics fires, not electrical fires, and fire extinguishers only should be used by those who
have received appropriate training. It is unnecessary and unacceptable to lock windows and
especially doors, which would block access by firefighters.
(QCMLS 2021: 7.8.5]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 7 · Question 129 · boc2 PDF page 215

question:
A technologist splashed a corrosive chemical in his/her eyes. To prevent permanent injury,
the first action should be to:
options: bandage the eyes and seek immediate emergency medical assistance
flush eyes with a chemical of opposite pH to neutralize the injury
use the eyewash station to flush eyes with water for 15 minutes
explanation:
The first action that should be taken is to use the eyewash station to flush eyes with water
for 15 minutes. Seeking medical assistance and bandaging the eyes are secondary, not
primary actions. Flushing eyes with any chemical is incorrect and completely unsafe.
[QCMLS 2021: 7.8.11.1]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 7 · Question 130 · boc2 PDF page 215

question:
A technologist spilled concentrated hydrochloric acid on his/her clothing and skin, affecting
a large portion of the body. After removing involved clothing, the next first aid treatment step
would be to:
options: use emergency safety shower and flush body with water
apply burn ointment to affected skin
pour baking soda on the skin and bandage
explanation:
After removing clothing, use the emergency safety shower and flush body with water to
stop the effects of acid. Seeking medical assistance is a secondary, not a primary first aid
action step. Applying baking soda or burn ointment are incorrect and not appropriate first aid
actions.
[QCMLS 2021: 7.8.11.1]

An automated CK assay gives a reading that is above the limits of linearity. A dilution of the
serum sample is made by adding 1 ml of serum to 9 ml of water. The instrument now reads
350 U/L. The correct report on the undiluted serum should be:

To correct for having used a dilution, multiply the answer obtained times the reciprocal of
the dilution made.

question:
A standard solution is a chemical solution that has a precisely known concentration. Standard
solution concentration is commonly expressed with which of the following units of measure:

To prepare a standard solution, a known mass of solute is dissolved, and the solution is

question:
A glucose determination was read on a spectrophotometer. The absorbance reading of the
standard was 0.30. The absorbance reading of the unknown was 0.20. The value of the
unknown is:

The value of the unknown is a ratio of the absorbance reading of the unknown to the
absorbance reading of the standard.
[Campbell 1997, p126]

question:
A technician is asked by the supervisor to prepare a standard solution from the stock
standard. What is the glassware of choice for this solution?
explanation:
Volumetric flasks are used to measure exact volumes and are primarily used in preparing
solutions of known concentrations.
[Tietz 2015, p116-117]

question: How many ml of red blood cells are to be used to make 25 ml of a 4% red cell suspension?
explanation:
The most commonly used equation for preparing suspension solutions is V1 x C1 = V2 x C2.
A 4% red cell suspension contains 4 ml of red cells per 100 ml (1 dl) of solution. Therefore,
(25) x (4) = (100) x (x). Solve for x.
[Kaplan 2003, p35]

question:
The volume of 25% stock sulfosalicylic acid needed to prepare 100 ml of 5% working solution
is:
explanation:
The most commonly used equation for preparing suspension solutions is V1 x C1 = V2 x C2.
In this case, (100) x (5) = (x) x (25). Solve for x.
[Kaplan 2003, p35]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 7 · Question 137 · boc2 PDF page 216

question:
To prepare 25 ml of 3% acetic acid, how much glacial acetic acid is needed?
J,tLS

V1 x C1 = V2 x C2. A 3% acetic acid solution contains 3 ml of acetic acid per
100 ml (1 dl) of solution. Therefore, (25) x (3) = (1 00)(x). Solve for x.

question: How many grams of sodium chloride are needed to prepare 1 l of 0.9% normal saline?
explanation:
This is a ratio calculation. 0.9% normal saline contains 0.9 g NaCl in 100 ml solution, ie,
0.9/100 = x/1000. Solve for xto determine how much NaCl is needed to prepare 1 l (1000 ml).
[Kaplan 2003, p35)

To prepare 40 ml of a 3% working solution, a technician would use what volume of stock
solution?
MLs

Therefore, (40) x (3) = (1 00)(x). Solve for x.
[Kaplan 2003, p35]

A technician is preparing a 75% solution. What volume of stock solution should be used to
prepare 8 ml?
1.1ts
explanation:

question:
Absorbance (A) of a solution may be converted to percent transmittance (% T) using
MLs
the formula:
explanation:
Absorbance, A, is a measure of the amount of light stopped, or absorbed, by a solution,
and the absorbance of light is a logarithmic function. Hence, the A scale is a logarithmic scale.
On the other hand, transmittance, T, is a measure of the amount of light allowed to pass
through a solution. Because the following relationship is true, A= light stopped and T = light
passed through, A and T are inversely related. They are also logarithmically related, because
the absorption of light is a logarithmic function.
[Campbell 1997, p212)

a compound fluoresces when it absorbs light at one wavelength and emits light at a

their ability to emit fluorescence after they have been incubated with fluorescent-labeled
monoclonal antibodies that bind to specific surface markers.

question:
Enzyme-multiplied immunoassay techniques (EMIT) differ from all other types of enzyme
immunoassays in that:
options: lysozyme is the only enzyme used to label the hapten molecule
no separation of bound and free antigen is required
inhibition of the enzyme label is accomplished with polyethylene glycol

antibody absorption to polystyrene tubes precludes competition to labeled and unlabeled
antigen
explanation:
Enzyme-multiplied immunoassay is a homogeneous enzyme immunoassay used to
quantitate drugs, hormone, etc. Unlike the heterogeneous assays, the free-labeled reactant

question:

antigens is correct?

the enzyme label is less stable than an isotopic label

the enzyme label is not an enzyme found naturally in serum
explanation:
Enzymes are one of the several labels used in labeled immunoassays. The catalytic
property of the enzyme is used to detect and quantitate the immunological reaction. Alkaline
phosphatase and horseradish peroxidase are examples of enzymes used. The product of the
enzymatic activity is monitored spectrophotometrically.

source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 7 · Question 255 · boc2 PDF page 233

question: Which of the following immunoassay labels offer the greatest detection limit?
explanation:
Chemiluminescent labels are based on the emission of light produced during a chemical
reaction. These labels are very useful because they provide very low levels of detection
(2 x 10-20 mol/L) with little or no background interference. Electrochemiluminescence differs
from chemiluminescence in that the reactive species that produce the chemiluminescent
reaction are electrochemically generated from stable precursors at the surface of an
electrode. With its use, detection limits of 200 fmol/L and a dynamic range extending over
6 orders of magnitude can be obtained.
[Clarke 2006, p122]

question: Which of the following is true regarding laboratory identification of mycobacteria?
options: rapid testing for tuberculosis is not available because the organism is slow-growing

automated systems can continuously monitor culture tubes for 6 weeks and report positive
results for culture
specimens must be kept at a low pH because the organisms are acid-fast

postive automated tests for tuberculosis no longer need to be reported because of low
incidence in the United States
explanation:
Direct nucleic acid amplification assays can detect Mycobacterium tuberculosis directly
from a patient specimen, with results available in less than 8 hours. Automated, continuously
monitoring culture systems for mycobacteria are available. Tubes are incubated for 6 weeks,
and positive tubes stained for acid-fast bacilli.
[QCMLS 2021: 6.2.1.3]

Which of the following is true of automated systems that can detect bacteria in the patient's
blood?
options: results are generally available in 2 to 3 days
specimens must be kept at 4°C from the time of collection until being run on the instrument

antibiotics taken by the patient before their dental procedure may be removed by the
device
flow cytometry is used to determine the bacterial count
explanation:

of positive blood cultures in 6-24 hours; some incorporate antimicrobial removal device that
absorbs any antibiotic present in patient's blood.
(QCMLS 2021: 6.7.1.5)

(RBC). Automated instruments determine the hematocrit using the directly measured MCV
and RBC count with the formula: MCV (fl) x RBC (x1012/L)/1000.

explanation:

new employees attain or regain a required level of knowledge and skill required to perform
a task or procedure. When a new method or new instrument is introduced to the laboratory,

question:
Staff competency needs to be assessed at which of the following times?
l,ILS
options:
when there is a temporary decrease in test volume that increases capacity to perform

competency assessment
when an employee's demonstrated competence does not meet criteria
explanation:
Competency assessment confirms a person's ability to use his or her skill and knowledge
to perform assigned duties correctly. It must be performed and documented for testing
personnel for each test or test system that an individual is authorized to perform before
reporting test results. Then, competency assessment should be performed semiannually
during the first year of testing, then annually; when methodology or instruments are changed;
when new test platforms are introduced; with newly hired, transferred, or promoted personnel;
and when an employee demonstrates repeated performance issues. A single mistake by an
employee would not trigger a need for staff competency assessment.
(QCMLS 2021: 7.4.2.10)

question:

adding 10 µL of serum to the first tube and then transferring 10 µL through each remaining
tube. What is the serum dilution of tube 7?
explanation:
A dilution involves the solute, the material being diluted and the diluent.

question:
Which of the these substances will not stimulate an immune response unless it is bound to a
larger molecule?
explanation:
A hapten is a small molecule that can act as antigen if it binds to a larger protein
molecule. Antigens, viruses and antibodies can stimulate an immune response on their
own depending on the context of stimulation. Adjuvants are compounds used to stimulate
the immune response to an antigen in a vaccine preparation. They do not directly serve
as antigens.
[QCMLS 2021: 8.1.3.2)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 8 · Question 81 · boc2 PDF page 284

question:
Blood is drawn from a patient for serological tests for a viral disease shortly after the time of
onset and again 4 weeks later. The results of the tests are considered diagnostic if the:
options: first antibody titer is 2x the second
first and second antibody titers are equal
first antibody titer is 4x the second
second antibody titer is at least 4x the first
explanation:
A 4-fold or greater increase in antibody titer from second of 2 serum specimens taken
from a patient during the acute and convalescent phases of an infection is considered to be
diagnostic.
[QCMLS 2021: 8.4.6)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 8 · Question 82 · boc2 PDF page 284

question:
The best method to detect infections due to rubella, Epstein-Barr and human
immunodeficiency viruses is:
explanation:
Serological tests are commonly used to detect antibodies in infections with viruses that
are difficult to culture, such as rubella, HIV, and EBV. EIA is a common serological method
because it is sensitive, specific, and can be automated.
(QCMLS 2021: 8.4.6) [Stevens 2017, p158-161)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 8 · Question 83 · boc2 PDF page 284

question: lmmunoassays are based on the principle of:
options: separation of bound and free analyte
explanation:
"Immunoassay" is a general term for an assay involving binding of an antibody to a
specific antigen.
[QCMLS 2021: 8.5.12)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 8 · Question 84 · boc2 PDF page 284

question:
What kind of antigen-antibody reaction would be expected if soluble antigen is added to
homologous antibody?
explanation:
By definition, precipitation involves combination of antigen and soluble antibody to form
insoluble complexes that fall out of solution.
[QCMLS 2021: 8.1.3) [Stevens 2017, p143)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 8 · Question 85 · boc2 PDF page 284

question:
In an indirect ELISA method designed to detect antibody to the rubella virus in patient serum,
the conjugate used should be:
options: anti-human lgG conjugated to an enzyme
anti-rubella antibody conjugated to an enzyme
rubella antigen conjugated to an enzyme
anti-rubella antibody conjugated to a substrate
explanation:
In an indirect ELISA, patient antibody to an antigen (eg, rubella antigen) is detected by
addition of an enzyme-labeled antibody to human immunoglobulin, which, in turn, binds to the
patient's lgG.
(QCMLS 2021: 8.5.12.2) [Stevens 2017, p159-160]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 8 · Question 87 · boc2 PDF page 285

question: In immunofixation electrophoresis:
options: the antibody reacts with the antigen and then the complex is electrophoresed
the antigen is electrophoresed into an antibody containing gel
the antigen is electrophoresed and then monospecific antisera is reacted with it

the antigen is electrophoresed, transferred to nitrocellulose and then antibody reacts with it
and an EIA is performed
explanation:
In immunoelectrophoresis, first the serum is separated in an agarose gel by
electrophoresis; then, in a trough that is cut parallel to the plane of the electrophoresis,
antiserum is placed. The antibody diffuses toward the serum proteins, and arcs of
antibody-antigen precipitation occur.
[QCMLS 2021: 8.1.3.6) [Stevens 2017, p144-146)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 8 · Question 88 · boc2 PDF page 285

question: A single test that could reliably detect neonatal infection in the absence of clinical signs is:
explanation:
An elevated lgM level indicates an in utero or neonatal infection.
[QCMLS 2021: 8.1.2.3) [Stevens 2017, p66-67]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 8 · Question 89 · boc2 PDF page 285

question:
The serological test that can be modified to selectively detect only specific lgM antibody in
untreated serum is:
explanation:
Indirect labeled assays can be designed to utilize class-specific antihuman
immunoglobulin, that is lgM specific.
[QCMLS 2021: 8.5.13) [Stevens 2017, p156-158)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 8 · Question 90 · boc2 PDF page 285

question: What is the immunologic method utilized in the flow cytometer?
explanation:
Flow cytometry uses fluorescent-labeled monoclonal antibodies to identify cells of interest
by binding to specific components within or on the surface of the cells.
[QCMLS 2021 : 8.5.15)
D. Complement
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 8 · Question 91 · boc2 PDF page 285

question: The assembly of the complement "membrane attack unit" is initiated with the binding of:
explanation:
In the complement cascade, the membrane attack unit begins with C5.
[QCMLS 2021: 8.1.4) (Stevens 2017, p93, 95)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 8 · Question 92 · boc2 PDF page 285

question:
Which of the following is most likely to activate the alternative pathway of complement
activation?
explanation:
Lipopolysaccharides initiate the alternative pathway of complement.
[QCMLS 2021: 8.1.4.2) [Stevens 2017, p19-20, 96-97)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 8 · Question 93 · boc2 PDF page 286

question: Which of the following is the larger residual split portion of C3?
explanation:
C3 breaks down to a small C3a, which floats away and is an anaphylatoxin. The larger
C3b, which lands on the target surface and becomes part of C5 convertase, is also a powerful
opsonin.
[QCMLS 2021: 8.1.4) [Stevens 2017, p94]
- - - - - -
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 8 · Question 94 · boc2 PDF page 286

question: Which of the following activities is associated with C3b?
explanation:
C3 breaks down to a small C3a, which floats away and is an anaphylatoxin. The larger
C3b, which lands on the target surface and becomes part of C5 convertase, is also a powerful
opsonin.
[QCMLS 2021: 8.1.4] [Stevens 2017, p94]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 8 · Question 95 · boc2 PDF page 286

question: Which of the following is the "recognition unit" in the classical complement pathway?
explanation:
Complement C1q is the recognition unit.
[QCMLS 2021: 8.1.4) [Stevens 2017, p94)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 8 · Question 96 · boc2 PDF page 286

question: Which of the following is the "membrane attack complex" of complement activation?
explanation:
Complement, C5-C9, is the membrane attack complex.
[QCMLS 2021 : 8.1.4) [Stevens 2017, p95-96]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 8 · Question 97 · boc2 PDF page 286

question: Which of the following releases histamine and other mediators from basophils?
explanation:
C3a, C4a and C5a are anaphylatoxins and cause release of histamine from basophils and
mast cells.
[QCMLS 2021: 8.1.4] [Stevens 2017, p102)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 8 · Question 98 · boc2 PDF page 286

question: Which of the following is not a mechanism involved in the complement cascade?
explanation:
Apoptosis is programmed cell death and is not involved in the complement cascade.
[QCMLS 2021: 8.1.4.2) [Stevens 2017, p279]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 8 · Question 99 · boc2 PDF page 286

question:
The activation mechanism of the alternative complement pathway is initiated differently from
that of the classical pathway because, in the alternative pathway:
options: antigen-antibody complexes containing lgM or lgG are required
C1 component of complement is involved
antigen-antibody complexes containing lgA or lgE may initiate activation
explanation:
lgA and lgE do not initiate the classical pathway of complement but can initiate the
alternative pathway.
[QCMLS 2021 : 8.1.4.2] [Stevens 2017, p92)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 8 · Question 100 · boc2 PDF page 286

question:
Which of the following is cleaved as a result of activation of the classical complement
pathway?
explanation:
Classical complement pathway: C1 is activated by binding 2 Fe fragments of
immunoglobulin, then C4 is split to C4a and C4b; C4b binds, and next C2 is bound and
cleaved; this forms C3 convertase, so C3 binds and is cleaved; C3b stays bound; C3a
floats away; C5 next is split and C5b binds and C5a floats away. C6, C7, C8, and C9 bind
sequentially and cause a hole in the membrane.
[QCMLS 2021: 8.1.4.1) [Stevens 2017, p94-95]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 8 · Question 101 · boc2 PDF page 286

question: The component associated only with the alternative pathway of complement activation is:
explanation:
Components unique to the alternative pathway include Factor 8, Factor D and properdin.
Properdin promotes the association of C3b with Factor 8.
[QCMLS 2021: 8.1.4.1] [Stevens 2017, p92-99)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 8 · Question 102 · boc2 PDF page 287

question:
Which of the following complement components is a strong chemotactic factor as well as a
strong anaphylatoxin?
explanation:
C5a is both chemotactic and an anaphylatoxin.
(QCMLS 2021 : 8.1.4.1] [Stevens 2017, p102)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 8 · Question 103 · boc2 PDF page 287

question: The C3b component of complement:
options: is a component of the C3 cleaving enzyme of the classical pathway
is cleaved by C3 inactivator into C3c and C3d
is not part of the alternative pathway
explanation:
C3 is a very powerful amplifying step of the classical and alterative pathways and also
forms a powerful opsinogen. Thus it must be subject to controls, and one such control is that
it can be broken down to C3c and C3d.
(QCMLS 2021 : 8.1.4.1] [Stevens 2017, p102-103]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 8 · Question 104 · boc2 PDF page 287

question: Components of the complement system most likely to coat a cell are:
explanation:
Conversion of C4 to C4a + C4b is an amplifying step with 30 molecules of C4 for every
molecule of C1; C3 conversion is a large amplifying step with about 200 molecules converted
for every C3 convertase. These extra molecules can bind to the cell surface.
(QCMLS 2021: 8.1.4] [Stevens 2017, p95-95]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 8 · Question 105 · boc2 PDF page 287

question:
Potent chemotactic activity is associated with which of the following components of the
complement system:
explanation:
C5a is a chemotaxin for neutrophils, basophils, mast cells and monocytes.
(QCMLS 2021: 8.1.4.1) [Stevens 2017, p102)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 8 · Question 106 · boc2 PDF page 287

question: Hereditary angioedema is characterized by:
options: decreased activity of C1 esterase inhibitor
increased activity of C1 esterase inhibitor
explanation:
C1 esterase inhibitor is associated with hereditary angioedema.
[QCMLS 2021 : 8.2.4.9] [Stevens 2017, p104)

question: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) patients often have which of the following test results?

question:
Systemic lupus erythematosus patients (SLE) with active disease often have which of the
following test results?
options: high titers of anti-smooth muscle antibodies
explanation:
CH50 is a good screening test for complement deficiencies in the classical pathway.
In SLE patients, the classical pathway is critical for immune complex clearance.
[QCMLS 2021: 8.2.1.15, 8.5.11.6)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 8 · Question 109 · boc2 PDF page 287

question:
Which of the following is decreased in serum during the active stages of systemic lupus
erythematosus (SLE)?
explanation:
C3 becomes depleted due to the autoantibody called C3-nephritic factor (C3NeF).
[QCMLS 2021: 8.2.1.15]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 8 · Question 110 · boc2 PDF page 288

question:
The ability of the immune system to recognize self-antigens versus nonself antigens is an
example of:
explanation:

question: The most rapid immediate hypersensitivity reaction is associated with:
explanation:

question:
A 2-year-old patient is suspected to have a peanut allergy because of breathing difficulties
(anaphylaxis), which progressed to wheezing within a few minutes upon consumption of
peanut butter. What in vitro diagnostic test (eg, solid-phase enzyme immunoassay (EIA]
or indirect ELISA) would confirm this type of allergy?
options: total serum lgG and allergen specific lgG
total serum lgA and allergen specific lgA
total serum lgE and allergen specific lgE
total serum lgM and allergen specific lgM
explanation:
Type I hypersensitivity, known as immediate-type hypersensitivity, is mediated by
lgE antibodies. Allergens bind lgE on the surface of mast cells, causing degranulation and
release of preformed mediators, including histamine, heparin, proteases, and chemotactic
factors. Common local or systemic reactions include fever, allergic asthma, hives, or
anaphylaxis. Common allergic triggering substances include peanuts, cow milk, eggs, pollen,
and penicillin. Type II hypersensitivity is antibody-mediated cellular cytotoxicity, mediated
by lgM & lgG antibodies. Common local or systemic reactions include rheumatic fever,
myasthenia gravis, Goodpasture syndrome, Graves disease, and multiple sclerosis. Common
triggering factors are anti cell surface antigen reactions in the health conditions including
blood transfusion reactions, erythroblastosis fetalis, various autoimmune diseases and early
transplant rejection. Type Ill hypersensitivity is mediated lgM & lgG antibodies that form
immune complexes and activate complement. Common local or systemic reactions and
health conditions include systemic lupus erythematosus, arthus reaction, and serum sickness.
Type IV hypersensitivity, or delayed-type hypersensitivity (0TH), is mediated by a T-cell
response to antigen. Antigens are generally either contact or intracellular. Contact antigens
includes inorganic chemicals, poison ivy, and nickel. Intracellular antigens can be located
on bacteria, fungi, parasites, or viruses. Transplant and tumor cell rejection are also 0TH.
Symptoms include local swelling and inflammation after initial sensitization phase of
1-2 weeks after first contact with antigen.
[QCMLS 2021 : 8.2.2)

is associated with a high incidence of icteric hepatitis

question:
Which laboratory technique is most frequently used to diagnose and follow the course of
therapy of a patient with secondary syphilis?
explanation:
Nontreponemal tests are used to screen for syphilis and monitor syphilis patients during
therapy. These tests, the VDRL and RPR, are based on the principle of flocculation, created
by the clumping of the fine cardiolipin particles used in the tests, after binding to patient's

question: Which of the following is true of the first stage of infection with Borrelia burgdorferi?
options: a generalized rash develops within 4-6 hours of a bite by a deer tick
the patient may be asymptomatic except for the rash
once developed, the rash persists for 7-1 O days
serologic testing is often positive within 1 week after the tick bite
explanation:
Borrelia burgdorferi is the causitive agent of Lyme disease transmitted to humans by a
deer tick bite. In the first stage of infection, most cases involve a localized rash, erythema
migrans, which appears between 2 days and 2 weeks after the bite. Patients may be
otherwise asymptomatic, and the rash fades within 3-4 weeks. Most first-stage patients are
negative on serologic testing, because the antibody response can take up to 6 weeks.
[QCMLS 2021: 8.4.3.1]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 8 · Question 173 · boc2 PDF page 296

question:
Which of the following is characteristic of the second stage of infection with
Borrelia burgdorferi?
MLs
options: spread to brain and spinal cord via cerebrospinal fluid
spread to multiple organ systems via the bloodstream
involvement of the liver, gallbladder, and pancreas
explanation:
Borrelia burgdorferi may spread to multiple organ systems via the bloodstream in the
second stage of infection. The first stage of infection lasts 3-6 weeks; without antibiotic
treatment, neurologic or cardiac involvement may develop in the second stage.
[QCMLS 2021: 8.4.3.1]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 8 · Question 174 · boc2 PDF page 296

question:
Which of the following is characteristic of the late stage of infection with Borrelia burgdorferi?
I.ILS
options: spread to brain and spinal cord via cerebrospinal fluid
development in patients refractory to antibiotic therapy
explanation:
The late stage of Borrelia burgdorferi infection occurs in a subset of untreated patients
months to years after infection. Symptoms are numerous and diverse, and arthritis, peripheral
neuropathy or encephalomyelitis may develop. Infection normally responds well to antibiotic
treatment even in the late stage.
(QCMLS 2021: 8.4.3.1)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 8 · Question 175 · boc2 PDF page 296

question:
Which of the following is consistent with CDC recommendations for confirmation of infection
with Borrelia burgdorferi?
options: perform screening EIA with comercially-prepared antibody coated slides
if asymptomatic but screening positive, perform both lgM and lgG western blot
confirm diagnosis if 1 of 3 critical lgM bands reactive on nitrocellulose strip
confirm diagnosis if half of the 10 critical lgG bands reactive on nitrocellulose strip
explanation:
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommend initial EIA or IFA
(using commercially prepared slides coated with antigen) followed by specific western blot
testing for confirmation of disease. If screening is positive or equivocal, lgG western blot
is indicated, and if signs or symptoms present for 30 days or less, lgM western blot also
indicated. In the western blot, nitrocellulose strips are reacted with patient serum to assess
antibody to specific Borrelia antigens. The CDC defines a positive reaction as at least 2
of 3 critical lgM bands reactive on the strip, and at least 5 of 10 critical lgG bands reactive
on the strip.
[QCMLS 2021 : 8.4.4]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 8 · Question 176 · boc2 PDF page 296

question:
Which of the following statements is most accurate regarding polymerase chain reaction
(PCR) confirmation of infection with Borrelia burgdorferi?
options: no cross-reactivity issues exist with PCR because of its specificity
PCR is recommended to routine positive screening tests
PCR can utilize either a fluorescent or enzyme marker
explanation:
Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for Borrelia burgdorferi detects genetic material from
the organism, and is very specific, with no cross-reactivity issues. It is used only when the
diagosis is very difficult, and not approved for routine testing.
[QCMLS 2021 : 8.4.4.4]

question:
The Quanti-FERON-TB Gold In-Tube (QFT-GIT) test to support diagnosis of latent
tuberculosis measures release of interferon gamma (IFNy) by:
explanation:
The Quanti-FERON-TB Gold In-Tube (QFT-GIT) assay measures IFNy produced
by T cells following stimulation with M. tuberculosis antigens. IFNy-producing T cells
are critical mediators of the cellular response to M. tuberculosis. Macrophages do not
produce I FNy; however, they are activated by this cytokine. Neutrophils are one of the
first cell types recruited to the site of inflammation or infection and are critical for control of
bacterial infections. They phagocytose and destroy pathogens, generally bacteria and fungi,
but do not secrete IFNy. B cells produce antibodies and present antigens to T cells, but
B cells do not produce IFNy.
[QCMLS 2021: 8.4.7.5]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 8 · Question 181 · boc2 PDF page 297

question: A cytokine that is classically associated with Th1 cells is:
explanation:
Interferon gamma (IFNy) is classically associated with Th1 cells. The Th1 response,
which results in generation of IFNy-producing T cells. This response is important for
cell-mediated immunity, which is typically directed against intracellular pathogens such as
mycobacteria. lnterleukin-4 is classically associated with a Th2 response that drives antibody
production. Interleukin 5 is associated with Th2 responses. Along with interleukin-4 and
interleukin-13, interleukin-5 drives eosinophil and lgE production. Interferon alpha is produced
by innate immune cells and is important for anti-viral defense.
[QCMLS 2021: 8.4.7.1]

question: Which of the following is true of Hashimoto thyroiditis?
options: it is more common in male patients
it is also known as chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis
anti-thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor (TRAb) is usually present
the goiter is firm rather than rubbery
explanation:
Hashimoto thyroiditis, also known as chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis, is the most common
autoimmune disease, affecting 0.8% of the population. It is characterized by a rubbery goiter,
TPO antibodies in 90% and Tg antibodies in 60-80%, but TRAb is not present. Hashimoto
thyroiditis is 5-10 times more prevalent in females than males.
[QCMLS 2021: 8.5.7.3)

question: Which of the following is true of Graves disease?
options: it is more common in male patients
it is also known as chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis
the presence of anti-thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor (TRAb) is diagnostic
the goiter is firm rather than rubbery
explanation:
Graves disease is common autoimmune disease characterized by a firm goiter, presence
of TRAb antibodies, and female predominance. However, the presence of TRAb is not
diagnosic by itself. TRAb antibody-binding assays involve competitive binding between a
labeleed TRAb reagend a patient antibody for TSH receptor.
[QCMLS 2021 : 8.5. 7 .4)

receptor stimulation.

question: The primary advantage of labeled immunoassays compared to unlabeled immunoassays is:

question:
A classic ELISA test is performed on a sample from a 67-year-old male patient who is
suspected of having ingested large amounts of drug X. The ELISA procedure is performed as
follows:
1. incubation of patient sample in antibody-coated microtiter plate wells
2. plate washing
3. addition of peroxidase-linked drug X conjugate
4. incubation followed by plate washing
5. addition of hydrogen peroxide
6. evaluation of color change
Which of the following is true regarding this procedure?
explanation:
Peroxidase is the enzyme that acts on hydrogen peroxide, which is the substrate.
The scenario describes a competitive assay because it uses patient antigen that competes
with the conjugate-linked reference antigen for binding to a specific antibody, which is on
the plate wells, not in the conjugate. Since plate washing occurs twice, the assay is not
homogenous, because heterogeneous assays require 1 or more steps of separation, where
unbound antibodies and/or unbound analyte must be washed away.
[QCMLS 2021 : 8.5.13] [Rittenhouse-Olson 2018, p110]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 8 · Question 215 · boc2 PDF page 302

question:
A physician suspects the presence of anti-lFNy autoantibodies in a patient. A serum sample
is sent to your laboratory to measure the presence or absence of anti-lFNy autoantibodies by
an enzyme-immunoassay. Which of the following would be used as the detecting reagent in
the kit?
options: horseradish peroxidase-conjugated mouse Ab to goat Ab
horseradish peroxidase-conjugated goat Ab to human IFNy
horseradish peroxidase-conjugated mouse Ab to human Ab
explanation:
Unconjugated recombinant human IFNy would be used as the capture reagent in
the assay. If the serum sample contains anti-lFNy autoantibodies, they will bind to the
recombinant human IFNy. To detect these bound antibodies (Ab), one needs to use a reagent
that will bind to human Ab. Therefore, the correct response is horseradish peroxidaseconjugated mouse Ab to human Ab.
[QCMLS 2021 : 8.5.13)

question: Flocculation tests for syphilis detect the presence of:

particles, small clumps are formed in a reaction called flocculation.
[QCMLS 2021: 8.4.2.2] [Stevens 2017, p374]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 8 · Question 219 · boc2 PDF page 302

question:
A serological test for syphilis that depends upon the detection of

source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 8 · Question 220 · boc2 PDF page 302

question: The serological test for syphilis recommended for detecting antibody in cerebrospinal fluid is:

question: Biological false-positive VDRL reactions are frequently encountered in patients with:

[QCMLS 2021: 8.4.2.2] [Stevens 2017, p374-375]

question:

question: For diagnosis of late latent or tertiary syphilis, the most appropriate assay is:
explanation:

question:
The air temperature throughout the serology laboratory is 20°C. How will this affect VDRL and
RPR test results?
options: no effect-the acceptable test range is 20-24°C
weaken reactions so that false-negatives occur
strengthen reactions so that positive titers appear elevated
increase the number of false-positives from spontaneous clumping
explanation:
It is recommended that the VDRL and RPR tests be performed at a temperature
of 23-29°C; optimal agglutination does not occur at temperatures below that range, resulting
in false-negative tests.
[Turgeon 2009, p219-222]

question:
What should be adjusted to make sure emission of fluorescence from a single fluorophore
does not bleed into multiple channels?
explanation:
The term "compensation," as it applies to flow cytometric analysis, refers to the process
of correcting for fluorescence spillover, ie, removing the signal of any given fluorochrome
from all detectors except the one devoted to measuring that dye. Because the fluorophores
used in flow cytometry emit photons of multiple energies and wavelengths, a mathematical
method called compensation was developed to address the measurement of the photons of
1 fluorophore in multiple detectors.
[QCMLS 2021 : 8.5.15)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 8 · Question 242 · boc2 PDF page 305

question: What does light emitted as FSC measure?
explanation:
In flow cytometry, the light scattered by cells is measured by 2 optical detectors: forward
scatter (FSC) that detects scatter along the path of the laser, and side scatter (SSC) which
measures scatter at a ninety-degree angle relative to the laser. FSC intensity is proportional
to the diameter of the cell, and is primarily due to light diffraction around the cell. FSC signal
can be used for the discrimination of cells by size. SSC, on the other hand, is from the light
refracted or reflected at the interface between the laser and intracellular structures, such as
granules and nucleus. SSC provides information about the internal complexity (ie, granularity)
of a cell.
[QCMLS 2021: 8.5.15]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 8 · Question 243 · boc2 PDF page 305

question: What type of biological sample is best measured by flow cytometry?
explanation:
Flow cytometry allows users to analyze single cells in a population. Single cells are
passed through the path of a laser and interrogated with various visible and fluorescent light
sources that allow users to assess a cell's size, granularity, and target protein composition.
[QCMLS 2021: 8.5.15.1]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 8 · Question 244 · boc2 PDF page 306

question: The process of centering the sample core within the sheath fluid is known as:
explanation:
Hydrodynamic focusing is a technique that enables users of flow cytometry cells to gauge
the size of particles in a flow channel, whether they are blood cells, viruses or bacteria.
A typical flow channel will be something as large as 2-3 mm in diameter down to a miniscule
50 µm. As particles enter the chamber, they will typically pass through a laser beam that
causes a temporary disruption in the optics. The size and nature of these disruptions are what
cause an instrument to be able to measure the particle's dimensions.
[QCMLS 2021: 8.5.15]

question:
To which filters do these definitions correspond: 1) transmit light in the specified wavelength,
2) transmit light equal to or longer than specified wavelength, 3) transmit light equal to or
shorter than specified wavelength
explanation:
Bandpass filters are optical filters that allow transmission of a specific range of
wavelengths, or band, while blocking other wavelengths. Many off-the-shelf bandpass filter
options are available, but when an application has specific requirements for bandwidth
or center wavelength not readily available, longpass and shortpass filters can be stacked
creating a customized bandpass filter. Longpass filters are optical filters that reflect short
wavelengths while transmitting, or passing, long wavelengths. Conversely, shortpass filters
transmit short wavelengths but reflect long ones.
[QCMLS 2021: 8.5.15] [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Band-pass_filter]

question:

immediately on his return home from vacation. Suspecting Lyme disease, his clinician ordered

health care provider then ordered follow-up testing with:
explanation:

are equivocal, ELISA is repeated. If the results are still equivocal, the next tier of testing is

question:
Mumps is diagnosed by swollen salivary glands, and it spreads from the infected person to
others through contact with saliva or respiratory secretions. Enzyme immunoassays (EIA) is
used to detect mump-specific antibodies to confirm current infection. Which of the following
results confirm mumps infection?
options:
detection of lgM antibodies within 3-4 days of onset of symptoms; detection of lgG
within 7-10 days and 4-fold increase in lgG between specimens collected in acute &
convalescence phases

detection of lgM antibodies within 5 days and rash; the detection of lgG within
10-14 days apart

detection of lgM antibodies with acute infection; detection of 4-fold increase in lgG between
acute & convalescent
detection of lgG at >6 months of age demonstrating post-birth infection
explanation:
Viral culture is the gold standard for detecting mumps, although molecular testing is
becoming the primary method. However, the confirmation of current infection is determined
when lgM antibodies can be detected within 3-4 days of onset of symptoms (negative result
does not rule out mumps infection}. lgG antibodies can be detected within 7-10 days; 4-fold
increase in lgG occurs between specimen collected in the acute phase, and a specimen
later collected in the convalescence phase. Rubella: Antibodies to rubella are detected on
hemagglutination inhibition, latex agglutination, or EIA. lgM or 4-fold rise in lgG titers in
samples collected 10-14 days apart indicates acute infection. lgM antibodies appear ~5 days
after onset of rash. Rubeola: EIA is used to test for measles antibodies to determine immune
status. lgM antibodies present with acute infection; 4-fold increase in lgG between acute
& convalescent sera. TORCH panel (toxoplasma, rubella, CMV, HSV): Infants tested at
>6 months of age for lgG antibodies demonstrate post-birth infection.
(QCMLS 2021 : 8.4.6]

question: Which of the following best correlates with a diagnosis of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)?
options: HEp-2 substrate IFA homogeneous pattern and antibodies to dsDNA (correct answer)
HEp-2 substrate IFA centromere pattern and antibodies to centromere B
HEp-2 substrate IFA speckled pattern and antibodies to Scl-70
HEp-2 substrate IFA speckled pattern and antibodies to SSB
explanation:
The presence of anti-dsDNA antibodies in association with a homogeneous pattern
using HEp-2 substrate IFA is classic for the diagnosis of SLE. HEp-2 substrate centromere
(centromere 8) and nucleolar (Scl-70) patterns are associated systemic sclerosis, while a
speckled pattern with SS-8 antibodies is frequently seen in Sjogren syndrome patients.
[QCMLS 2021: 8.2.1.15, 8.5.6)

question:
A 54-year-old female previous smoker presents with a recent history of fever, swollen joints,
and morning stiffness. Laboratory results indicate elevated C-reactive protein, positive cyclic
citrullinated peptide of 205 units (cut-off: 20 units), speckled ANA pattern (titer 1 :320), and
negative rheumatoid factor. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Of the autoimmune diseases listed, only rheumatoid arthritis (RA) has the strongest
association with smoking and positivity for cyclic citrullinated protein/peptide antibodies.
RA can occur with or without the presence of rheumatoid factor, and ANA can sometimes be
positive. Reactive arthritis is generally due to an infection.
[QCMLS 2021: 8.2.1.13, 8.5.8)
